source_paragraphs: Let $W=\langle s,t\mid s^2=t^2=1\rangle$ be the infinite dihedral Coxeter group, so $S=\{s,t\}$ and $m(s,t)=\infty$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (3)(c),(4)). Then:

**(1) Growth series.** Every word reduces by canceling adjacent equal generators to an alternating word. For each $q\ge1$, the two alternating words $(st)^q$ and $(ts)^q$ have length $2q$; for each $q\ge0$, $(st)^qs$ and $(ts)^qt$ have length $2q+1$. These words are reduced by [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (7), with the generators interchanged for the words beginning with $t$; their pairwise distinctness is proved in step 1.1 below using the infinite order of $st$ from (4). They exhaust the nonidentity elements, so $W$ has one element of length $0$ and exactly two of each length $n\ge1$:
$$P_W(t)=1+2t+2t^2+2t^3+\cdots=1+\frac{2t}{1-t}=\frac{1+t}{1-t}\in\mathbb Q(t)$$
The coefficientwise identity $(1-t)P_W=1+t$ follows from the displayed coefficients by the Cauchy product ([[def-formal-power-series-and-coefficient-extraction]]), and $1-t$ has unit constant term ([[thm-formal-power-series-unit-criterion]], [[def-rational-formal-power-series-and-reduced-denominator]]).
[L1] For $m(s,t)=\infty$ the rank-two product $st$ has infinite order in $W$ and the elements $s,t\in W$ are distinct involutions ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (3)(c),(4)).

[L2] Every alternating word beginning with either $s$ or $t$ of length $q\ge1$ is reduced in the ambient group (apply the source also with $s,t$ interchanged) ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (7)).
source_use_steps: 1.1 Every word in $s,t$ can be shortened by canceling an adjacent pair $ss$ or $tt$ by [L3], so a shortest word is alternating. For each $q\ge1$ the two alternating words of length $2q$ are $(st)^q,(ts)^q$, and for each $q\ge0$ the two of length $2q+1$ are $(st)^qs,(ts)^qt$. They are reduced by [L2], so unequal lengths give unequal elements. Put $r=st$, so $ts=r^{-1}$ and $t=r^{-1}s$. At the same even length $2q>0$, equality of the two words would give $r^q=r^{-q}$ and hence $r^{2q}=1$; at the same odd length $2q+1$, equality would give $r^qs=r^{-q}t=r^{-q-1}s$ and hence $r^{2q+1}=1$. Both contradict the infinite order in [L1]. Equivalently, the presentation admits the parity homomorphism sending both generators to $-1$, because each defining relator has even length, so even and odd words cannot coincide. Every element has one of these forms or is the identity. Thus $[t^0]P_W=1$ and $[t^n]P_W=2$ for every $n\ge1$. By the Cauchy-product definition, $(1-t)P_W=1+t$: its coefficients are $1$ at degree $0$, $2-1=1$ at degree $1$, and $2-2=0$ at every degree $n\ge2$. Since $1-t$ has unit constant term, $P_W=(1+t)/(1-t)$ in $\mathbb Z\llbracket t\rrbracket$, and [L4] makes this a rational series. [L1, L2, L3, L4, L9, algebra]

2.1 A subset $I\subseteq S$ is spherical exactly when $W_I$ is finite. The three proper parabolics $W_\emptyset=\{1\}$, $W_{\{s\}}=\{1,s\}$ and $W_{\{t\}}=\{1,t\}$ are finite; $W_S=W$ is infinite by [L1]. Thus the spherical subsets are exactly $\emptyset,\{s\},\{t\}$, with $P_{W_\emptyset}=1$ and $P_{W_{\{s\}}}=P_{W_{\{t\}}}=1+t$, while all four subsets occur in the Steinberg sum of [L6]. Substituting $P_W=(1+t)/(1-t)$ from step 1.1 gives $1-2/(1+t)+1/P_W=1-2/(1+t)+(1-t)/(1+t)=0$, the infinite case of [L6]. [step 1.1, L1, L6, algebra]

2.2 In $\mathbb Q(t)$, $P_W(t^{-1})=(1+t^{-1})/(1-t^{-1})=-P_W(t)$. If $t^{N}P_W(t^{-1})=P_W(t)$ for some $N\ge0$, then $-t^NP_W(t)=P_W(t)$; since $P_W\ne0$, this forces $t^N=-1$, impossible in $\mathbb Q(t)$. Thus no such $N$ exists. The alternating words in step 1.1 have unbounded lengths, so $W$ has no longest element; the infinite-case statement of [L7] also says no element has all descents. [step 1.1, L1, L7, L8, algebra]

citations.quote: one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$

7. **Ambient reducedness of dihedral words.** Let $s\ne t$, $m:=m(s,t)$, and for $q\ge1$ let $w_q$ be the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$. If $m<\infty$ and $q\le m$, or if $m=\infty$ and $q\ge1$, then $\ell(w_q)=q$, every word in $S$ representing $w_q$ has length at least $q$, and $w_1,\dots,w_q$ are pairwise distinct.

source_paragraphs:
Let $S=\{s,t\}$ with $m(s,t)=\infty$, so that $W=\langle s,t\rangle$ is the
infinite dihedral group with length $\ell$
([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]); put $u:=st$, so that $u$ has
infinite order, $W=\{u^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{u^ks:k\in\mathbb Z\}$,
$sus^{-1}=u^{-1}$, and $\ell(u^k)=2|k|$ for every $k$, while $\ell(u^ks)=2|k|+1$
for $k\ge0$ and $\ell(u^ks)=2|k|-1$ for $k\le-1$
([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (3)(c), (4) and (7): the
alternating words representing these elements are reduced). Let $I=\{s\}$ and
$J=\{t\}$, so that $W_I=\{1,s\}$, $W_J=\{1,t\}$ and
$W_I\cap W_J=W_\emptyset=\{1\}$
([[thm-cg-parabolic-intersections-and-coset-factorization]] (1)); these are the
*standard* parabolics of rank $1$.

[F1] $st$ has infinite order in $W$ and $s\ne t$; alternating words in $s,t$ are reduced in the ambient group, so the value of an alternating word of length $q\ge1$ beginning with $s$ or with $t$ has length exactly $q$ ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]).
source_use_steps:
1.2 *The one-sided quotients.* Every element of $W$ is $u^m$ or $u^ms$ with $m\in\mathbb Z$: any word in $s,t$ can be shortened by cancelling adjacent equal letters until it alternates, and an alternating word is $(st)^m$, $(ts)^m$, $(st)^ms$ or $(ts)^ms$, which is $u^m$, $u^{-m}$, $u^ms$ or $u^{-m}s$. The two families are disjoint: if $u^m=u^{m'}s$ then $s=u^{m-m'}\in\langle uangle$, and $s=u^k$ implies $u^{-k}=su^ks=s\cdot s\cdot s=s=u^k$, where the first equality uses $sus^{-1}=u^{-1}$ and $s=s^{-1}$, so $u^{2k}=1$ and $k=0$ by the infinite order of $u$, whence $s=1$ and $st=t$ of order $2$, contradicting [F1]. Using the reduced alternating forms of [F1]: for $m\ge1$ one has $s\,u^m=s(st)^m=t(st)^{m-1}$ of length $2m-1<2m$, so $u^m
otin{}^IW$; for $m<0$ the element $s\,u^m=(st)^{|m|}s$ is alternating of length $2|m|+1>2|m|=\ell(u^m)$, and for $m=0$ one has $s\cdot1=s$ of length $1>0$, so no left descent occurs for $m\le0$; for $m\ge0$ one has $s(u^ms)=u^{-m}$ of length $2m<2m+1=\ell(u^ms)$, so $u^ms
otin{}^IW$; and for $m\le-1$ the element $s(u^ms)=u^{-m}$ has length $2|m|>2|m|-1=\ell(u^ms)$, so no left descent occurs. Hence ${}^IW=\{u^m:m\le0\}\cup\{u^ms:m\le-1\}=\{u^{-k}:k\ge0\}\cup\{u^{-k}s:k\ge1\}$. Dually, for $m\ge1$ one has $u^mt=(st)^{m-1}s$ of length $2m-1<2m$, so $u^m
otin W^J$; for $m\le0$ the element $u^mt=(ts)^{|m|}t$ is alternating of length $2|m|+1>2|m|=\ell(u^m)$, so no right descent occurs; for $m\ge0$ one has $u^mst=u^{m+1}$ of length $2m+2>2m+1=\ell(u^ms)$, so $u^ms\in W^J$; and for $m\le-1$ the element $u^mst=u^{m+1}$ has length $2|m|-2<2|m|-1=\ell(u^ms)$, so $u^ms
otin W^J$. Hence $W^J=\{u^m:m\le0\}\cup\{u^ms:m\ge0\}$. [F1, F2]

2.1 *The blocks of the decomposition.* For $k\ge0$ put $d_k:=(ts)^k=u^{-k}$. Then $s(ts)^k=(st)^ks=u^ks$, since $s\,t\,s=sts$ may be rewritten as $(st)s$; further $(ts)^kt=(ts)^{k+1}s=u^{-(k+1)}s$, and $s(ts)^kt=(st)^{k+1}=u^{k+1}$. Hence $W_I(ts)^kW_J=\{u^{-k},u^ks,u^{-(k+1)}s,u^{k+1}\}$, and by the reduced alternating forms of [F1] these four elements have lengths $2k$, $2k+1$, $2(k+1)-1=2k+1$ and $2k+2$; they are pairwise distinct, the two translations having different lengths and the two $s$-multiples being equal only if $u^{2k+1}=1$, impossible by [F1]. The minimum length among them is $2k=\ell(d_k)$, and $d_k=u^{-k}\in{}^IW^J$ by the description of step 1.2, so [F4] shows that $d_k$ is the unique minimum of the double coset $W_I(ts)^kW_J$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.2]

2.2 *The two-sided quotient.* By step 1.2, ${}^IW^J={}^IW\cap W^J$ consists of the elements of the list $\{u^m:m\le0\}\cup\{u^ms:m\le-1\}$ that also lie in the list $\{u^m:m\le0\}\cup\{u^ms:m\ge0\}$. Since the two families are disjoint, an element of the first family lies in the second list precisely when its index already satisfies $m\le0$, and an element of the second family would have to satisfy $m\le-1$ (for ${}^IW$) and $m\ge0$ (for $W^J$) simultaneously, which is impossible. Hence ${}^IW^J=\{u^m:m\le0\}=\{u^{-k}:k\ge0\}=\{(ts)^k:k\ge0\}$. [F1, F2, step 1.2]

3.1 *The intersection, the sizes and the decomposition.* For $k\ge0$ one has $d_k^{-1}sd_k=u^ksu^{-k}=u^{2k}s$ because $su^{-k}s=u^{k}$; the only element of $I$ is $s$, and $u^{2k}s\in J=\{1,t\}$ would force $u^{2k}s=t=u^{-1}s$, hence $u^{2k}=u^{-1}$ and $u^{2k+1}=1$, impossible since $u$ has infinite order by [F1]. Hence $K=\emptyset$, $W_K=\{1\}$ and $W_I^K=W_I$; the size formula of [F4] gives $|W_I(ts)^kW_J|=2\cdot2=4=2\cdot2/1$. Finally each element of $W$ is $u^m$ or $u^ms$ with a unique $m\in\mathbb Z$, and the four families $u^{-k}(k\ge0)$, $u^{k+1}(k\ge0)$, $u^ks(k\ge0)$ and $u^{-(k+1)}s(k\ge0)$ list exactly $u^m$ for $m\le0$, $u^m$ for $m\ge1$, $u^ms$ for $m\ge0$ and $u^ms$ for $m\le-1$, without repetition by the disjointness of the two families in step 1.2. Hence $W$ is the disjoint union of the double cosets $W_I(ts)^kW_J$, $k\ge0$, the first block being $W_IW_J=\{1,s,t,st\}$; this completes the example. [F1, F4, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2] ∎

[F3] If $m(s,t)=\infty$ then $st$ has infinite order in $W$ and $s\ne t$, and the alternating words in $s,t$ are reduced in the ambient group: the value of an alternating word of length $q\ge1$ has length exactly $q$ ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]).
source_use_steps: 1.2 *The subgroup $H'$.* Put $u:=st$. Every word in $s,t$ can be shortened by cancelling adjacent equal letters $ss$ or $tt$ until it alternates, so an alternating word is $(st)^k$, $(ts)^k$, $(st)^ks$ or $(ts)^ks$ for some $k\ge0$; since $(ts)^k=u^{-k}$ and $(ts)^ks=u^{-k}s$, we get $W=\{u^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{u^ks:k\in\mathbb Z\}$, a normal form in which the two families are distinguished by the parity homomorphism below. Since $s=s^{-1}$ and $t=t^{-1}$ we have $sus^{-1}=s(st)s=ts=u^{-1}$ and hence $su^{2m}s=u^{-2m}$ for all $m$. In particular $tst=t(st)t\cdot t=(ts)^2s=u^{-2}s$, so $tst$ is a reflection by [F4], and $tst=u^{-2}s\in\langle s,u^2\rangle$; conversely $s\cdot(u^{-2}s)=su^{-2}s=u^{2}$ and $(u^{-2}s)\cdot s=u^{-2}$, so $\langle s,tst\rangle=\langle s,u^2\rangle$. The set $S_0:=\{u^{2k}:k\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{u^{2k}s:k\in\mathbb Z\}$ is closed under multiplication: the four product types use $su^{2m}s=u^{-2m}$ and give $u^{2k}u^{2m}=u^{2(k+m)}$, $u^{2k}s\cdot u^{2m}s=u^{2(k-m)}$, $u^{2k}\cdot u^{2m}s=u^{2(k+m)}s$ and $u^{2k}s\cdot u^{2m}=u^{2(k-m)}s$; it contains $s=u^0s$ and $u^2$, and each of its elements is a product of $s$ and $u^2$; hence $S_0=\langle s,u^2\rangle=H'$. The assignment $s\mapsto0$, $t\mapsto1$ sends the relators $s^2$ and $t^2$ to $0$, so by [F5] it defines a homomorphism $\varphi\colon W\to\mathbb Z/2$; by [F6], $\varphi(u^k)=k\bmod2$ and $\varphi(u^ks)=k\bmod2$, so the set $H_0:=\{w:\varphi(w)=0\}$ equals $\{u^{2k}:k\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{u^{2k}s:k\in\mathbb Z\}=S_0=H'$, and since $\varphi(t)=1$ the complement of $H_0$ is the single coset $H_0t$; hence $H'$ has exactly two cosets in $W$, of which it is one, so it has index $2$. Since $u$ has infinite order by [F3], $W$ is infinite and $H'$, of index $2$, is infinite as well. [F3, F4, F5, F6, algebra]

2.2 *$H'$ is not parabolic.* By [F2] the parabolic subgroups of $W$ are the conjugates of $W_\emptyset=\{1\}$, $W_{\{s\}}=\{1,s\}$, $W_{\{t\}}=\{1,t\}$ and $W_{\{s,t\}}=W$. The subgroups $\{1\}$ and $W$ are their own conjugates; the conjugates of $\{1,s\}$ or of $\{1,t\}$ are the subgroups $\{1,r\}$ with $r\in T$, and conversely every $r\in T$ is a conjugate of the simple reflection $s$ or of the simple reflection $t$ by [F4], so the conjugates of these two standard parabolics are exactly the subgroups $\{1,r\}$, $r\in T$. By step 1.2 the group $H'$ contains $s$, and $s
eq1$ because $s=1$ would force $st=t$ to have order $2$, against [F3]; further $H'$ is infinite and has index $2$ in $W$, so $t
otin H'$ (indeed $\varphi(t)=1$) and $H'
eq W$. Hence $H'$ is none of $\{1\}$, of the two-element subgroups $\{1,r\}$, or of $W$: $H'$ is a reflection subgroup that is not parabolic, and the inclusion "parabolic $\subsetneq$ reflection subgroup" is strict. [F2, F3, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

**Given:** The Coxeter matrix on $S=\{s,t\}$ with $m(s,t)=3$; the presented group $W$ with its length $\ell$ of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; the reflection set $T$, the prefix reflections, the sign-change sets $\Phi(w)$ and the exact order of $st$ from [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]; the exchange and deletion statements of [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]]; and the length table for $I_2(3)$ of [[ex-hh-finite-dihedral-reduced-words]].

In $W$ one has $s^2=1$, so $s\cdot st=s^2t=t$; and $\ell(t)=1$ by [F1]. Hence $\ell(s\cdot st)=1=2-1$ and [F2] (2) applies to the reduced word $(s_1,s_2)=(s,t)$ with the letter $s$: there is $i\in\{1,2\}$ with $s\cdot st=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_2$. Since $s\cdot st=t$ and the two deletion words are $\widehat{s_1}s_2=t$ and $s_1\widehat{s_2}=s$, only $i=1$ gives the value $t$, so $s\cdot st=\widehat{s_1}s_2=t$: the predicted deletion is the deletion of the first letter. 1.2 **The prefix reflections and the repeated one.** Compute the prefix reflections of $(s,t,s,t)$ from $r_i=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}$ with $w_0=1$, $w_1=s$, $w_2=st$, $w_3=sts$: $r_1=s$; $r_2=s\,t\,s=sts$; $r_3=(st)\,s\,(st)^{-1}=sts\cdot ts=ststs=(st)^2s=ts\cdot s=t$, where $(st)^{-1}=ts$ and $(st)^2=(st)^{-1}$ because $st$ has order $3$ [F1, F4]; and $r_4=(sts)\,t\,(sts)=s\,t\,s\,t\,s\,t\,s=(st)^3s=s$, using $(st)^3=1$ and $s^2=t^2=1$ [F5]. 1.3 **The deletion and the value identity.** Since $r_1=r_4$, [F1] (6)(a) with $i=1$, $j=4$ gives $stst=\widehat{s_1}t s\widehat{s_4}=ts$. Independently, $(st)^2=(st)^{-1}$ because $st$ has order $3$ [F1], and $(st)^{-1}=t^{-1}s^{-1}=ts$ [F4]; hence $stst=(st)^2=ts$, confirming that deleting the first and the last letter of $(s,t,s,t)$ preserves the value. [F1, F4]

2.1 **The element and its reflection set.** By step 1.3 the word $(s,t,s,t)$ represents $stst=ts$ and has length $4$, while $\ell(stst)=\ell(ts)=2$ by [F3] with $m=3$, $k=2$ and $k=1$; hence the word is not reduced. By [F1] (6)(b) the function $\eta(r,stst)=(-1)^{n(r)}$ is expression-independent, so it may be computed from the word $(s,t,s,t)$ with the prefix reflections of step 1.2: of these $r_1=r_4=s$ occurs twice and $r_2=sts$, $r_3=t$ occur once each, so $\Phi(stst)=\{r\in T:\eta(r,stst)=-1\}=\{sts,\,t\}$ has cardinality $2=\ell(stst)$, in agreement with the cardinality forced for any reduced expression by [F1] (6)(c); in particular $s
otin\Phi(stst)$, and the two-letter deletion licensed by [F1] (6)(a) is the one deleting the equal reflections $r_1=r_4$, not an arbitrary pair of equal letters. The last point: deleting the letters at positions $1$ and $3$ of $(s,t,s,t)$ leaves the word $(t,t)$ with value $t^2=1$ [F5], and $1
e ts$ since $\ell(1)=0
e2=\ell(ts)$; so that deletion does not preserve the value. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.2]

1. **Involutions.** $\sigma_s^2=\mathrm{id}_E$ for every $s\in S$; each $\sigma_s$ is invertible, and $\ell(s)=1$.
2. **The rank-two block.** For any distinct $s,t\in S$, put $m:=m(s,t)$, $c:=c_{st}$, $P:=\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)\subseteq E$, $A:=\sigma_s\sigma_t$ and $B:=A|_P$. Then $A(P)\subseteq P$, and in the basis $(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$,
$$B(\alpha_s)=(c^2-1)\alpha_s+c\,\alpha_t,\qquad B(\alpha_t)=-c\,\alpha_s-\alpha_t;\qquad \operatorname{tr}(B)=c^2-2,\qquad \det(B)=1 .$$
Moreover $A(v)-v\in P$ for every $v\in E$. Consequently $E=P\oplus Q$ with $Q:=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_u:u\in S,\ u\notin\{s,t\}\}$, and for every $v=p+q$ with $p\in P$, $q\in Q$ and every $k\ge1$,
$$A^k(p+q)=B^k p+\bigl(\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{k-1}\bigr)\bigl(A(q)-q\bigr)+q .$$
3. **Exact order of the rank-two product.** For any distinct $s,t$ and the notation of (2), when $m<\infty$ put $\zeta:=\zeta_{st}$, of order $2m$, so $c=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$; when $m=\infty$ use $c=2$, with no $\zeta$ stipulated. Then:
   (a) if $2<m<\infty$, the characteristic polynomial of $B$ is $X^2-(c^2-2)X+1=(X-\zeta^2)(X-\zeta^{-2})$ with distinct roots; $B$ is diagonalisable, $B^m=\mathrm{id}_P$, $\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{m-1}=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for $0<k<m$;
   (b) if $m=2$, then $c=0$ and $B=-\mathrm{id}_P$;
   (c) if $m=\infty$, then $c=2$, $B\ne\mathrm{id}_P$, $(B-\mathrm{id}_P)^2=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for every $k\ge1$.
   Hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=A$ has order exactly $m$ when $m<\infty$, and infinite order when $m=\infty$; in particular $A^m=\mathrm{id}_E$ and $A^k\ne\mathrm{id}_E$ for $0<k<m$ in the finite case.
4. **The representation and the exact dihedral orders.** The assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ respects every defining relator of $W$ and induces a unique homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ with $\sigma(s)=\sigma_s$. Consequently, for any distinct $s,t\in S$, one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$).
5. **The signed reflection action.** Let $T:=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}\subseteq W$. For $s\in S$ define $U_s:\{\pm1\}\times T\to\{\pm1\}\times T$ by
$$U_s(\varepsilon,r):=\bigl(\varepsilon\cdot(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},\ srs\bigr),$$
where $\delta(s,r)=1$ if $r=s$ and $\delta(s,r)=0$ otherwise. Then $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ for every $s$, and the assignment $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s:=U_s(\varepsilon,r)$ extends to a well-defined **right action** of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ (so $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot1=(\varepsilon,r)$ and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(wv)=((\varepsilon,r)\cdot w)\cdot v$). Indeed the only relations to check are $s^2=1$ and, for distinct $s,t$ with $m=m(s,t)<\infty$, $(st)^m=1$: $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ because for $r=s$ the two signs cancel while for $r\ne s$ one has $srs\ne s$ and $U_s(\varepsilon,srs)=(\varepsilon,r)$; and the alternating word $s\,t\,s\,t\cdots$ of length $2m$ acts trivially because its $2m$ prefix reflections $r_i:=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}$ (with $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$) satisfy $r_{i+m}=r_i$ for $1\le i\le m$ and $r_1,\dots,r_m$ are pairwise distinct, so each reflection of the dihedral subgroup $\langle s,t\rangle$ occurs exactly twice and every accumulated sign is even while the conjugating coordinate returns to $r$ because $(st)^m=1$.
6. **Prefix reflections, deletion and expression independence.** Let $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ be a word in $S$ with value $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and prefix reflections $r_i=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1$, and let $n(r):=\#\{i:r_i=r\}$.
   (a) If $r_i=r_j$ for some $i<j$, then $s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots\widehat{s_j}\cdots s_k=w$: the two letters $s_i,s_j$ can be deleted.
   (b) $(-1)^{n(r)}=:\eta(r,w)$ depends only on $w$ and $r$, and the right action satisfies $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\,\eta(r,w),\,w^{-1}rw)$.
   (c) If the word is reduced ($k=\ell(w)$), then $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $r$, the map $i\mapsto r_i$ is injective, and the set $\Phi(w):=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r\in T:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ is independent of the reduced expression chosen, with $\#\Phi(w)=\ell(w)$.

source_paragraphs: Let $m\ge2$, $S=\{s,t\}$ and $m(s,t)=m$, so that $W=\langle s,t\mid s^2=t^2=(st)^m=1\rangle$ is dihedral of order $2m$ by [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (4).

**Given:** A group $W$ presented by the Coxeter matrix on $S=\{s,t\}$ with $m(s,t)=m\ge2$, with the length function $\ell$ of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]; the exact order of $st$ and the ambient reducedness of alternating words from [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]; the deletion statement of [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]]; and the vocabulary of powers and orders.

[F2] [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (1),(4): "$\sigma_s^2=\mathrm{id}_E$ for every $s\in S$; each $\sigma_s$ is invertible, and $\ell(s)=1$"; and "Consequently, for any distinct $s,t\in S$, one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$).".

[F3] [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (7): "Let $s\ne t$, $m:=m(s,t)$, and for $q\ge1$ let $w_q$ be the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$. If $m<\infty$ and $q\le m$, or if $m=\infty$ and $q\ge1$, then $\ell(w_q)=q$, every word in $S$ representing $w_q$ has length at least $q$, and $w_1,\dots,w_q$ are pairwise distinct."
source_use_steps: 1.2 **Reducedness of alternating words.** Let $1\le q\le m$ and let $w_q$ be the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$; by [F3], $\ell(w_q)=q$ and every word in $S$ representing $w_q$ has length at least $q$, so that alternating word is reduced, and $w_1,\dots,w_q$ are pairwise distinct. The same statements hold for alternating words beginning with $t$: interchanging the roles of $s$ and $t$ preserves every hypothesis, since $m(t,s)=m(s,t)=m$ and the presentation is symmetric in $s,t$ [F1]. [F1, F3]

2.1 **Distinctness.** If $(st)^k=(st)^l$ with $0\le k<l<m$, then $(st)^{l-k}=1$ with $0<l-k<m$, contradicting the exact order $m$ of $st$ [F2, F5]. If $(st)^ks=(st)^ls$ with $0\le k<l<m$, then multiplying on the right by $s$ gives $(st)^k=(st)^l$, the previous case. If finally $(st)^k=(st)^ls$, then $(st)^{k-l}=s$, so $s\in\langle st\rangle$ and also $t=s\cdot st\in\langle st\rangle$, whence $W=\langle st\rangle$ is cyclic and therefore abelian; then $st=ts$, so $(st)^2=stst=s(ts)t=s(st)t=(ss)(tt)=1$, and the order of $st$ divides $2$. Since that order is $m\ge2$ by [F2], this forces $m=2$, in which case $\langle st\rangle=\{1,st\}$ while $s\in\{1,st\}$ gives $s=1$ or $t=1$; both are impossible because $\ell(s)=\ell(t)=1$ [F2]. Hence no rotation equals a reflection and the $2m$ elements of step 1.1 are pairwise distinct, so they exhaust $W$ and $|W|=2m$. [F2, F5, step 1.1]

source_use_steps: 1.1 **The group and its two elements.** The relation $s^2=1$ holds in $W$ because $s^2\in R\subseteq N$ [F1]. Every element of $W$ is the image of a product of the generator $s$ and its inverse, and $s^{-1}=s$ in $W$, so every element is a power $s^k$ with $k\ge0$; since $s^k$ is $1$ for even $k$ and $s$ for odd $k$, one has $W=\{1,s\}$. By [F1] $\ell(1)=0$ and by [F3] $\ell(s)=1$, so $s\ne1$, and the bijection $W\to\mathbb{Z}/2$ with $1\mapsto0$, $s\mapsto1$ is a homomorphism; hence $W\cong\mathbb{Z}/2$. [F1, F3]

2.1 **Word values and reduced words.** A word $(s,\dots,s)$ of length $k$ has value $s^k$, which is $1$ for even $k$ and $s$ for odd $k$ by step 1.1; in particular $(\;)$ has value $1$ and $(s)$ has value $s$ with lengths $0=\ell(1)$ and $1=\ell(s)$ [F1, F3], so both are reduced. If $k\ge2$, the word of length $k$ has value of length at most $1<k$, so it is not reduced; by [F4] it admits a deletion of two letters with the same value, and iterating this deletion, the length drops by two each time until the word has length $\ell(1)$ or $\ell(s)$, namely until it is $(\;)$ or $(s)$. Hence the only reduced words are $(\;)$ and $(s)$. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.1]

3.1 **Reflections, roots and the signed action.** Since $W$ is abelian and $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$, the reflection set is $T=\{s\}$ [F3, step 1.1]. By [F3] the group generated by $\sigma_s$ is $\{1,\sigma_s\}$, so the root set of [F2] is $\Phi=\{\alpha_s,\sigma_s(\alpha_s)\}=\{\alpha_s,-\alpha_s\}$, and these two vectors are distinct: $\alpha_s=-\alpha_s$ would give $2\alpha_s=0$, while the basis vector $\alpha_s$ is nonzero and $\operatorname{char}K=0$ [F2]. For $r=s$ the formula of [F3] gives $(\varepsilon,s)\cdot s=U_s(\varepsilon,s)=(\varepsilon(-1)^{\delta(s,s)},sss)=(-\varepsilon,s)$, and this action is faithful by [F4]. [F2, F3, F4] ∎

citations.quote: Then $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ for every $s$, and the assignment $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s:=U_s(\varepsilon,r)$ extends to a well-defined **right action** of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ (so $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot1=(\varepsilon,r)$ and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(wv)=((\varepsilon,r)\cdot w)\cdot v$).

source_paragraphs: [F3] Alternating dihedral words are reduced in the ambient group: for $q\le m$ the alternating word of length $q$ has length exactly $q$ in $W$. ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]])
source_use_steps: 2.1 Let $m=2k+1$ be odd and let $\xi:=(st)^ks$, the alternating word of length $m$; by [F3] $\ell(\xi)=m$, and $s\xi=s(st)^ks=(ts)^k=(st)^{-k}=(st)^{k+1}$ while $\xi t=(st)^kst=(st)^{k+1}$, the middle identities using $(st)^{-1}=ts$ and the relator $(st)^m=1$ together with $m-k=k+1$ (the values here are elements of $W$, not literal words). Put $z:=s\xi=\xi t$; then $z$ is the alternating element of length $m-1$, so $\ell(s\xi)=\ell(\xi t)=\ell(z)=m-1=\ell(\xi)-1$ by [F3], while $s\xi t=zt=(st)^{k+1}t=(st)^kstt=(st)^ks=\xi$ gives $\ell(s\xi t)=\ell(\xi)$. This is configuration (v) of 1.1 at the weight $\xi$, so $P_sQ_t(e_\xi)-Q_tP_s(e_\xi)=(u_t-u_s)e_z$ with $z=\xi t$ the alternating element of length $m-1$; for $m=3$ this is the displayed identity with $z=ts$. The difference vanishes in $E$ if and only if $u_t-u_s=0$ in the coefficient ring, because $(e_w)$ is a basis. Consequently independent parameters with $u_s\ne u_t$ violate the commutation of the length operators, while $u_s=u_t$ holds exactly when the quadratic relations of $T_s$ and $T_t$ coincide ([F1]); the identity $v_t(u_t-u_s)=(v_t-v_s)(v_t+v_s^{-1})$ shows that $u_s=u_t$ is equivalent to $(v_t-v_s)(v_t+v_s^{-1})=0$, since $v_t$ is a unit. For unit-valued specializations into an integral domain this holds exactly when $v_t=v_s$ or $v_t=-v_s^{-1}$ by [F5]; over a ring with zero divisors only the product-zero condition is asserted. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

source_paragraphs: [F5] There is a homomorphism $\operatorname{sgn}:W\to\{\pm1\}$ with $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$ and $\operatorname{sgn}(w)=(-1)^{\ell(w)}$ for all $w\in W$; hence $\ell(ws)=\ell(w)\pm1$ for all $w\in W$ and $s\in S$. Also $\ell(s)=1$ for every $s\in S$, so $s\ne1$ in $W$. Distinct generators are distinct in $W$, the product $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$, the standard parabolic subgroup $W_{s,t}$ is the Coxeter system presented by the restricted matrix on $\{s,t\}$ with intrinsic length $\ell_{s,t}$ equal to $\ell$ on $W_{s,t}$, and every right coset $W_{s,t}a$ has a unique minimal-length representative $d$, characterized by $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$ and satisfying $\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ for all $u\in W_{s,t}$ ([[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], [[thm-hh-coxeter-exchange-deletion-and-faithfulness]], [[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]]).

[F6] For $s\ne t$ and $q\ge1$, if $m(s,t)<\infty$ and $q\le m(s,t)$, or if $m(s,t)=\infty$, then the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$ has length $q$ in $W_{s,t}$ ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]); the same holds for the alternating word beginning with $t$.
source_use_steps: 1.1 **Set-up.** For the rank-two calculation fix $s\ne t$ in $S$ and adopt the notation of [F1] and [F3]. For $r\in S$ the sets $B_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)>0\}$ and $rB_r=\{f\in V^*:f(e_r)<0\}$ are disjoint and $C^\circ=\bigcap_{r\in S}B_r$; the dual action satisfies $v(B_s\cap B_t)=\{v\cdot f:f\in B_s\cap B_t\}$, and the action of $v\in W_{s,t}$ on $V^*$ is linear. By [F5] the intrinsic length satisfies $\ell_{s,t}(x)=\ell(x)$ for $x\in W_{s,t}$. [F1, F3, F5, given]

1.4 **The finite dihedral group.** Assume $m:=m(s,t)<\infty$ and write $u:=st$. Since $u^m=1$ by [F5], the set $\{u_0,\dots,u_{2m-1}\}$ is closed under right multiplication by $s$ and $t$: indeed $u_{2j}s=u_{2j+1}$ and $u_{2j+1}s=u_{2j}$ for $2j<2m$; $u_{2j}t=u_{2j-1}$ for $j\ge1$; $u_0t=u_{2m-1}$ because $(st)^{m-1}s=(st)^{-1}s=(ts)s=t$; and $u_{2j+1}t=u_{2j+2}$ for $2j+1<2m$, $u_{2m-1}t=1$. Since $W_{s,t}$ is generated by $s,t$ and contains $1$, it equals $\{u_0,\dots,u_{2m-1}\}$. The $u_k$ are pairwise distinct: if $u_j=u_k$ with $j<k<2m$, then $1=u_j^{-1}u_k$; for $j,k$ of equal parity this equals $u^{\pm(k-j)/2}$ with $0<(k-j)/2<m$, contradicting the exact order $m$ of $u$ from [F5], while for parities differing it equals $s\,u^{p}$ or $u^{p}s$ with $2|p|<2m$, so it would give $u^{p}=s$, impossible because $\operatorname{sgn}(u^{p})=1$ while $\operatorname{sgn}(s)=-1$. Hence $|W_{s,t}|=2m$, the $u_k$ are distinct, $u_{k+2m}=u_k$, and the pairs $u_k,u_{k+1}$ and $u_{2m-1},u_0$ are edges of the Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for the generating set $\{s,t\}$. That graph is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ because $x
e xs$ and $xs
e xt$ for all $x$ (as $s
e1$ and $s
e t$ by [F5]); it therefore *is* the displayed $2m$-cycle, so $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=\min(k,2m-k)$ is the graph distance from $u_0$. Moreover $su_k=u_{\sigma(k)}$ and $tu_k=u_{	au(k)}$ with $\sigma(k)\equiv1-k\pmod{2m}$ and $	au(k)\equiv-1-k\pmod{2m}$ for $0\le k<2m$: these are $s(st)^{j}=u^{-j}s$, $t(st)^{j}=u^{-j}t=u^{-j-1}s$ applied to $u_{2j}=u^{j}$ and $u_{2j+1}=u^{j}s$, together with the case $k=0$. [F5, F6, algebra]

1.5 **The infinite dihedral group.** Assume $m(s,t)=\infty$, write $u:=st$, and let $u'_k$ be the alternating word of length $k$ beginning with $t$. By [F5], $u$ has infinite order, and by [F6] $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k=\ell_{s,t}(u'_k)$ for all $k\ge0$. The union $X:=\{u_k:k\ge0\}\cup\{u'_k:k\ge0\}$ is closed under right multiplication by $s$ and $t$ ($u_{2j}s=u_{2j+1}$, $u_{2j+1}s=u_{2j}$, $u_{2j}t=u_{2j-1}$ for $j\ge1$, $u_0t=u'_1$, $u_{2j+1}t=u_{2j+2}$, symmetrically for $u'_k$), so $X=W_{s,t}$; by [F6] the elements $u_k$ are pairwise distinct with $\ell_{s,t}(u_k)=k$ for every $k\ge0$, and likewise the $u'_k$. The Cayley graph of $W_{s,t}$ for $\{s,t\}$ is connected, and every vertex has degree exactly $2$ (as in 1.4), so it is the two-way infinite path $\cdots u'_2,u'_1,1,u_1,u_2\cdots$, and the graph distance from $1$ to $u_k$, or to $u'_k$, equals $\ell_{s,t}$ of that element, namely $k$. On the affine line $\{f\in P^*:f(e_s+e_t)=1\}$, parametrized by $y_s$, the generators act by $s:y_s\mapsto-y_s$ and $t:y_s\mapsto 2-y_s$ by [F3] (here $c=1$); consequently the affine map of $u_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s-2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s-2j$ for $k=2j+1$, and that of $u'_k$ is $y_s\mapsto y_s+2j$ for $k=2j$ and $y_s\mapsto-y_s+2j+2$ for $k=2j+1$, by induction on $k$ (each step composes with $s$ or $t$ alternately). Hence the trace of $u_kC_P^\circ$ is the interval $(-k,-k+1)$ and that of $u'_kC_P^\circ$ is $(k,k+1)$. Since these intervals are pairwise distinct, an element of $W_{s,t}=X$ is determined by the trace of its chamber. Writing $v_j$ $(j\in\mathbb Z)$ for the element with trace $(j,j+1)$, namely $v_j=u_{-j}$ for $j\le0$ and $v_j=u'_j$ for $j\ge0$, one therefore has $\ell_{s,t}(v_j)=|j|$ together with $s\cdot v_j=v_{-j-1}$ and $t\cdot v_j=v_{1-j}$, because the affine maps send the interval $(j,j+1)$ to $(-j-1,-j)$, respectively $(1-j,2-j)$. [F3, F5, F6, algebra]

5.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm P)$. ** Fix $n\ge0$ and suppose only $(\mathrm Q_n)$. If $S$ is empty there is no $s$ to check. If $S=\{s\}$ then $W=\{1,s\}$ by $s^2=1$ and [F5], and the only positive-length chamber is $sC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$, with $\ell(s)=1$, proving $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$ directly. Now suppose $|S|\ge2$. First $(\mathrm Q_n)$ and (1) imply $(\mathrm P_n)$: for any $a$ of length $n$ and generator $r$, choose $q\ne r$ and use $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to write $a=ud$, with $aC^\circ\subseteq u(B_r\cap B_q)$ and $n=\ell_{r,q}(u)+\ell(d)$. The rank-two dichotomy gives the positive alternative or the negative alternative with $\ell_{r,q}(ru)=\ell_{r,q}(u)-1$; in the latter case $\ell(ra)\le\ell_{r,q}(ru)+\ell(d)=n-1$, hence equality by [F5]. This is $(\mathrm P_n)$. Let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and let $s\in S$; choose $t$ with $w=tw'$ and $\ell(w')=n$. If $s=t$, then $(\mathrm P_n)$ applied to $w'$ gives $w'C^\circ\subseteq B_s$: the second alternative would give $\ell(sw')=\ell(w')-1=n-1$, whereas $\ell(sw')=\ell(w)=n+1$ here. Hence $wC^\circ=t(w'C^\circ)\subseteq tB_s=sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(w')=n=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. If $s\ne t$, apply $(\mathrm Q_n)$ to $w'$: there is $u\in W_{s,t}$ with $w'C^\circ\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w')=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w')$. Put $v:=tu\in W_{s,t}$. If $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$, then $wC^\circ\subseteq tu(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq B_s$. Otherwise $v(B_s\cap B_t)\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell_{s,t}(sv)=\ell_{s,t}(v)-1$ by (1) from 4.1, so with $d:=u^{-1}w'$ one has $wC^\circ\subseteq sB_s$ and $\ell(sw)=\ell(stu\,d)\le\ell_{s,t}(stu)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(sv)-1+\ell(d)\le\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(d)=\ell(w')=\ell(w)-1$, while $\ell(sw)\ge\ell(w)-1$ by [F5]; hence $\ell(sw)=\ell(w)-1$, the second alternative of $(\mathrm P_{n+1})$. [step 4.1, F3, F5, algebra]

6.1 **The conditional step for $(\mathrm Q)$. ** Suppose $(\mathrm Q_n)$ and $(\mathrm P_m)$ for all $m\le n+1$, as in the second conditional implication of (2), and let $w\in W$ with $\ell(w)=n+1$ and $s\ne t$. By [F5] factor $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_{s,t}$ and $d$ the minimal representative of $W_{s,t}w$; then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ and $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$. Since $\ell(d)\le n+1$, $(\mathrm P_{\ell(d)})$ is available: it is part of the stated supposition. Applying it to $d$ and $s'\in\{s,t\}$, the second alternative would give $\ell(s'd)=\ell(d)-1$, contradicting $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$; hence $dC^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$. Therefore $wC^\circ=u(dC^\circ)\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$ and $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w)$, which is $(\mathrm Q_{n+1})$. [step 5.1, F5, algebra]

8.1 **Part (3).** Let $w\in W$ and $s\ne t$, and factor $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_{s,t}$ and $d$ the minimal representative of $W_{s,t}w$. By [F5], $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$ and $\ell(s'd)>\ell(d)$ for $s'\in\{s,t\}$; since $\ell(d)\le\ell(w)$, $(\mathrm P_{\ell(d)})$ from 7.1 applies to $d$, and the second alternative would give $\ell(s'd)=\ell(d)-1$, a contradiction; hence $dC^\circ\subseteq B_s\cap B_t$ and $wC^\circ=u(dC^\circ)\subseteq u(B_s\cap B_t)$, with $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)=\ell_{s,t}(u)+\ell(u^{-1}w)$ because $u^{-1}w=d$ and $\ell_{s,t}(u)=\ell(u)$. [step 7.1, F5, algebra]

citations.quote:
1. **Involutions.** $\sigma_s^2=\mathrm{id}_E$ for every $s\in S$; each $\sigma_s$ is invertible, and $\ell(s)=1$.
2. **The rank-two block.** For any distinct $s,t\in S$, put $m:=m(s,t)$, $c:=c_{st}$, $P:=\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)\subseteq E$, $A:=\sigma_s\sigma_t$ and $B:=A|_P$. Then $A(P)\subseteq P$, and in the basis $(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$,
$$B(\alpha_s)=(c^2-1)\alpha_s+c\,\alpha_t,\qquad B(\alpha_t)=-c\,\alpha_s-\alpha_t;\qquad \operatorname{tr}(B)=c^2-2,\qquad \det(B)=1 .$$
Moreover $A(v)-v\in P$ for every $v\in E$. Consequently $E=P\oplus Q$ with $Q:=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_u:u\in S,\ u\notin\{s,t\}\}$, and for every $v=p+q$ with $p\in P$, $q\in Q$ and every $k\ge1$,
$$A^k(p+q)=B^k p+\bigl(\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{k-1}\bigr)\bigl(A(q)-q\bigr)+q .$$
3. **Exact order of the rank-two product.** For any distinct $s,t$ and the notation of (2), when $m<\infty$ put $\zeta:=\zeta_{st}$, of order $2m$, so $c=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$; when $m=\infty$ use $c=2$, with no $\zeta$ stipulated. Then:
   (a) if $2<m<\infty$, the characteristic polynomial of $B$ is $X^2-(c^2-2)X+1=(X-\zeta^2)(X-\zeta^{-2})$ with distinct roots; $B$ is diagonalisable, $B^m=\mathrm{id}_P$, $\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{m-1}=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for $0<k<m$;
   (b) if $m=2$, then $c=0$ and $B=-\mathrm{id}_P$;
   (c) if $m=\infty$, then $c=2$, $B\ne\mathrm{id}_P$, $(B-\mathrm{id}_P)^2=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for every $k\ge1$.
   Hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=A$ has order exactly $m$ when $m<\infty$, and infinite order when $m=\infty$; in particular $A^m=\mathrm{id}_E$ and $A^k\ne\mathrm{id}_E$ for $0<k<m$ in the finite case.
4. **The representation and the exact dihedral orders.** The assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ respects every defining relator of $W$ and induces a unique homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ with $\sigma(s)=\sigma_s$. Consequently, for any distinct $s,t\in S$, one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$).

7. **Ambient reducedness of dihedral words.** Let $s\ne t$, $m:=m(s,t)$, and for $q\ge1$ let $w_q$ be the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$. If $m<\infty$ and $q\le m$, or if $m=\infty$ and $q\ge1$, then $\ell(w_q)=q$, every word in $S$ representing $w_q$ has length at least $q$, and $w_1,\dots,w_q$ are pairwise distinct. Thus dihedral alternating words are reduced in the ambient group $W$, not merely inside $\langle s,t\rangle$.

source_paragraphs: [F3] Alternating dihedral words are reduced in the ambient group: if $s\ne t$ and $w_q$ is the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$, then $\ell(w_q)=q$ whenever $q\le m(s,t)$ with $m(s,t)<\infty$. ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]])
source_use_steps: 3.1 Let $s\ne t$ with $m:=m(s,t)<\infty$, and put $a:=P_sP_tP_s\cdots$ and $b:=P_tP_sP_t\cdots$, each product having $m$ alternating factors. Let $w_1$ be the alternating product of $m$ factors beginning with $s$ and $w_2$ that beginning with $t$. Each successive factor is length-increasing along the alternating word by [F3] (the partial alternating words of length $\le m$ are reduced), so the computation of 1.5 gives $a(e_1)=e_{w_1}$ and, with the roles of $s,t$ exchanged, $b(e_1)=e_{w_2}$. In $W$ one has $w_1=w_2$: since $(st)(ts)=s\,t\,t\,s=s^2=1$ in $W$, we have $(ts)=(st)^{-1}$ ([F5]), and the relator $(st)^m=1$ gives $(st)^{-k}=(st)^{m-k}$ for $0\le k\le m$; hence if $m=2k+1$ then $w_2=(ts)^kt=(st)^{-k}t=(st)^{k+1}t=(st)^ks=w_1$, while if $m=2k$ then $w_2=(ts)^k=(st)^{-k}=(st)^k=w_1$. Now let $w=u_1\cdots u_k$ be any reduced expression. By 1.5, $Q_{u_k}\cdots Q_{u_1}(e_1)=e_w$, and by 2.1 every $P_s$ commutes with every $Q_t$, so $a(e_w)=aQ_{u_k}\cdots Q_{u_1}(e_1)=Q_{u_k}\cdots Q_{u_1}a(e_1)=Q_{u_k}\cdots Q_{u_1}b(e_1)=b(e_w)$; since $(e_w)_{w\in W}$ is a basis, $a=b$ ([F6]). The same argument with $P$ replaced by $Q$ throughout gives the braid relations for the $Q$'s. [F3, F5, F6, step 1.5, step 2.1]

source_paragraphs: [F4] The reflection set carries the right action $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s=U_s(\varepsilon,r)=(\varepsilon\cdot(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},\,srs)$ of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$, and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\,\eta(r,w),\,w^{-1}rw)$ for a well-defined sign $\eta(r,w)\in\{\pm1\}$ depending only on $w$ and $r$; for a reduced word with prefix reflections $r_i$ one has $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$, the map $i\mapsto r_i$ is injective, and $\Phi(w):=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r\in T:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ is independent of the reduced expression and has cardinality $\ell(w)$ ([[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]).
source_use_steps: 1.1 **Set-up.** Fix a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_n$ of an element $w\in W$, write $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$ and $r_i:=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}\in T$ for the prefix reflections, and note $\rho(w_j)=\rho(s_1)\cdots\rho(s_j)$ by [F6] and $\rho(r_i)=\rho(w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1})=r_{\rho(w_{i-1})e_{s_i}}$. [F1, F4, F6, given]

1.4 **The shorteners are exactly the prefix reflections.** Keep the reduced expression of 1.1 and let $r\in T$. If $r=r_i$ is a prefix reflection of the word, then $r_iw=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}w_{i-1}s_is_{i+1}\cdots s_n=w_{i-1}s_{i+1}\cdots s_n=s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots s_n$, so $\ell(r_iw)<n=\ell(w)$; and by [F4] the set $\{r_1,\dots,r_n\}$ equals $\Phi(w)=\{r:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ and its members are pairwise distinct. Conversely let $r\in T$ with $\ell(rw)<\ell(w)$ and suppose $\eta(r,w)=+1$. The formula of [F4] implies the cocycle identity $\eta(x,uv)=\eta(x,u)\eta(u^{-1}xu,v)$ for all $x\in T$, $u,v\in W$: indeed $(\varepsilon,x)\cdot(uv)=((\varepsilon,x)\cdot u)\cdot v$, and comparing first coordinates of the displayed formula gives the identity. With $x=r$, $u=r$, $v=w$ this gives $\eta(r,rw)=\eta(r,r)\eta(r,w)=\eta(r,r)$; also $\eta(r,1)=1$, since the action of $1$ is the identity. We claim $\eta(r,r)=-1$. Write $r=usu^{-1}$ with $s\in S$, $u\in W$, so that $u^{-1}ru=s$; applying the action formula of [F4] successively along the word $usu^{-1}$ to $(\varepsilon,r)$ gives $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot u=(\varepsilon\eta(r,u),u^{-1}ru)=(\varepsilon\eta(r,u),s)$, then $U_s(\varepsilon\eta(r,u),s)=(-\varepsilon\eta(r,u),s)$ by the definition of $U_s$ in [F4], and then $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(usu^{-1})=(-\varepsilon\eta(r,u)\eta(s,u^{-1}),r)$. Comparing with $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot r=(\varepsilon\eta(r,r),r)$ from [F4] yields $\eta(r,r)=-\eta(r,u)\eta(s,u^{-1})$. Applying the cocycle identity with $x=s$, $u=u^{-1}$, $v=u$ gives $\eta(s,1)=\eta(s,u^{-1})\eta(usu^{-1},u)$, that is $1=\eta(s,u^{-1})\eta(r,u)$; hence $\eta(r,r)=-\eta(r,u)^2=-1$ under the supposition $\eta(r,w)=+1$. Therefore $\eta(r,rw)=-1$, so $r\in\Phi(rw)=\{x\in T:\eta(x,rw)=-1\}$; by [F4] applied to the shorter element $rw$, the element $r$ is one of the prefix reflections of a reduced expression of $rw$, and the first paragraph of this step applied to that element gives $\ell(r\cdot rw)<\ell(rw)$, that is $\ell(w)<\ell(rw)$, contradicting $\ell(rw)<\ell(w)$. Hence $\eta(r,w)=-1$ and $r\in\Phi(w)=\{r_1,\dots,r_n\}$. Thus $\{r\in T:\ell(rw)<\ell(w)\}=\{r_1,\dots,r_n\}$. [F4, algebra]

citations.quote:
5. **The signed reflection action.** Let $T:=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}\subseteq W$. For $s\in S$ define $U_s:\{\pm1\}\times T\to\{\pm1\}\times T$ by
$$U_s(\varepsilon,r):=\bigl(\varepsilon\cdot(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},\ srs\bigr),$$
where $\delta(s,r)=1$ if $r=s$ and $\delta(s,r)=0$ otherwise. Then $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ for every $s$, and the assignment $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s:=U_s(\varepsilon,r)$ extends to a well-defined **right action** of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ (so $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot1=(\varepsilon,r)$ and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(wv)=((\varepsilon,r)\cdot w)\cdot v$). Indeed the only relations to check are $s^2=1$ and, for distinct $s,t$ with $m=m(s,t)<\infty$, $(st)^m=1$: $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ because for $r=s$ the two signs cancel while for $r\ne s$ one has $srs\ne s$ and $U_s(\varepsilon,srs)=(\varepsilon,r)$; and the alternating word $s\,t\,s\,t\cdots$ of length $2m$ acts trivially because its $2m$ prefix reflections $r_i:=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}$ (with $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$) satisfy $r_{i+m}=r_i$ for $1\le i\le m$ and $r_1,\dots,r_m$ are pairwise distinct, so each reflection of the dihedral subgroup $\langle s,t\rangle$ occurs exactly twice and every accumulated sign is even while the conjugating coordinate returns to $r$ because $(st)^m=1$.
6. **Prefix reflections, deletion and expression independence.** Let $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ be a word in $S$ with value $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and prefix reflections $r_i=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1$, and let $n(r):=\#\{i:r_i=r\}$.
   (a) If $r_i=r_j$ for some $i<j$, then $s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots\widehat{s_j}\cdots s_k=w$: the two letters $s_i,s_j$ can be deleted.
   (b) $(-1)^{n(r)}=:\eta(r,w)$ depends only on $w$ and $r$, and the right action satisfies $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\,\eta(r,w),\,w^{-1}rw)$.
   (c) If the word is reduced ($k=\ell(w)$), then $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $r$, the map $i\mapsto r_i$ is injective, and the set $\Phi(w):=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r\in T:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ is independent of the reduced expression chosen, with $\#\Phi(w)=\ell(w)$.

source_paragraphs: Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, $W$ the presented group, $\ell$ its length function, and let $T$, $\eta$, $\Phi$ and the right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ be as in [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]].

**Given:** A finite Coxeter matrix $(S,m)$, the presented group $W$ with its length $\ell$, the reflection set $T$ and the right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ of [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and a word $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ in $S$ in each claim below.

[F2] [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]: the right action of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ defined by $U_s(\varepsilon,r)=(\varepsilon(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},srs)$ satisfies $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\,\eta(r,w),w^{-1}rw)$ with $\eta(r,w)=(-1)^{n(r)}$ depending only on $w$ and $r$; $T=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}$; for a reduced expression $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ with prefix reflections $r_i=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1$ one has $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $r$, the map $i\mapsto r_i$ is injective, and $\Phi(w):=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r\in T:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ is independent of the reduced expression, with $\#\Phi(w)=\ell(w)$; also $\ell(s)=1$ for every $s\in S$.

source_paragraphs: Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix; let $W$ and $\ell$ be the presented group and its length and let $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ be the geometric representation, as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], with reflection set $T$ and sign-change sets $\Phi(w)$ as in that lemma; and let $s\ne t$ in $S$ with $m:=m(s,t)$.

[F3] [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]]: the assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ induces a homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$; $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$); the right action satisfies $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\eta(r,w),w^{-1}rw)$ with $\eta(r,w)$ depending only on $w$ and $r$; for a reduced word with prefix reflections $r_i=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1$ one has $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$ for all $r$ and $\Phi(w)=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ independent of the reduced expression, of cardinality $\ell(w)$; the prefix reflections of the alternating word $(a,b,a,b,\dots)$ with $a=s_1,b=s_2$ are $r_i=(ab)^{i-1}a$; and an alternating word of length $q\le m$, or of any length when $m=\infty$, is reduced in $W$, its value having length $q$.

1.1 **The dihedral subgroup and the singleton claim.** Put $r:=st$. By [F3], $r$ has order exactly $m$ when $m<\infty$ and infinite order when $m=\infty$, and $srs=s(st)s=(ss)(ts)=ts=r^{-1}$; hence $sr^k=r^{-k}s$ for every $k$ by induction on $k$. It follows that $D:=\langle s,tangle$ is exactly the set $D_0:=\{r^k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\cup\{r^ks:k\in\mathbb Z\}$: indeed $D_0$ contains $s=r^0s$ and $t=r^{-1}s$ (as $r^{-1}s=(ts)s=t$), and $D_0$ is closed under multiplication, since $r^a\cdot r^b=r^{a+b}$, $r^a\cdot r^bs=r^{a+b}s$, $r^as\cdot r^b=r^a(sr^b)=r^ar^{-b}s=r^{a-b}s$ and $r^as\cdot r^bs=r^a(sr^b)s=r^ar^{-b}ss=r^{a-b}$; so $D_0$ is a subgroup containing $s$ and $t$, while every product of copies of $s,t$ lies in $D_0$ by this closure, whence $D=D_0$. The elements $r^k$ and $r^ks$ with $0\le k<m$ (all $k\in\mathbb Z$ when $m=\infty$) are pairwise distinct: $r^k=r^l$ with $0\le k<l<m$ gives $r^{l-k}=1$, impossible by minimality of the order $m$, while for $m=\infty$ the powers $r^k$ with $k\in\mathbb Z$ are distinct because $r$ has infinite order; and $r^k=r^ls$ gives $r^{k-l}=s$, so $s\in\langle rangle$, which cannot happen because $s\in\langle rangle$ would make $s$ commute with $r$, giving $t=sr=rs=sts$, hence $st=ts$ and $r=r^{-1}$; then $r^2=1$, so the order of $r$ divides $2$, an impossibility unless $m=2$, and in the case $m=2$ one has $\langle rangle=\{1,r\}$ with $s
eq1$ and $s
eq r=st$ (the latter would give $t=1$). Hence $D$ has exactly $2m$ elements and is dihedral when $m<\infty$, and is infinite dihedral when $m=\infty$. Next, $P:=\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$ is preserved by $\sigma_s$ and $\sigma_t$, and $\sigma_s(v)-v\in P$ and $\sigma_t(v)-v\in P$ for every $v\in E$: on the basis, $\sigma_s(\alpha_s)-\alpha_s=-2\alpha_s$, $\sigma_s(\alpha_t)-\alpha_t=c_{st}\alpha_s$ and $\sigma_s(\alpha_u)-\alpha_u=c_{su}\alpha_s$ for $u
otin\{s,t\}$, and symmetrically for $\sigma_t$. So for every product $g$ of copies of $\sigma_s,\sigma_t$ one has $g(v)-v\in P$ for all $v$ by induction on the number of factors, and therefore every element of $D=\langle s,tangle$ acts as the identity on $E/P$. If $u\in S\setminus\{s,t\}$, then $\alpha_u
otin P$ because the basis is linearly independent, while $\sigma_u(\alpha_u)=-\alpha_u$, so $\sigma_u(\alpha_u)-\alpha_u=-2\alpha_u
otin P$ and $\sigma_u$ does not act as the identity on $E/P$; since $\sigma$ is a homomorphism, $u
otin D$. Hence $S\cap D=\{s,t\}$. Finally, every element of $D$ has a reduced expression with letters in $\{s,t\}$: for $0\le k<m$ the element $r^k$ equals both $(st)^k$ and $(ts)^{m-k}=r^{k-m}$, alternating words of lengths $2k$ and $2(m-k)$ whose minimum is at most $m$, and the element $r^ks$ equals both $(st)^ks$ and $(ts)^{m-k-1}t$ (for $k=0$ the first is the single letter $s$), alternating words of lengths $2k+1$ and $2(m-k)-1$ whose minimum is at most $m$; an alternating word of length at most $m$ is reduced in $W$ by [F3], so the shorter of the two is a reduced expression of the element in the letters $\{s,t\}$. When $m=\infty$ every alternating word is reduced by [F3], and $r^k$ with $k<0$ is written as $(ts)^{-k}$ and $r^ks$ with $k<0$ as $(ts)^{-k-1}t$. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.2 **Braid moves preserve the value.** Let $m=m(s,t)<\infty$ and let $L_m$ and $L'_m$ be the two alternating words of length $m$ in $\{s,t\}$, beginning with $s$ and with $t$. With $r:=st$ of order $m$ by [F3], one has $L_m=(st)^{m/2}=r^{m/2}$ and $L'_m=(ts)^{m/2}=r^{-m/2}$ when $m$ is even, so their values coincide; and $L_m=(st)^{(m-1)/2}s=r^{(m-1)/2}s$ while $L'_m=t(st)^{(m-1)/2}=(ts)^{(m-1)/2}t=r^{-(m-1)/2}t=r^{-(m-1)/2}r^{-1}s=r^{-(m+1)/2}s=r^{(m-1)/2}s$ when $m$ is odd, using $ts=r^{-1}$, $t=r^{-1}s$ and $r^m=1$. Hence replacing an alternating subword of length $m$ by the other alternating word of the same length leaves the value in $W$ unchanged, and so does a finite sequence of such replacements. [F1, F3, algebra]

1.3 **The reduction step.** Let $q\ge2$ and let $\mathbf a=(a_1,\dots,a_q)$ and $\mathbf b=(b_1,\dots,b_q)$ be reduced words for the same element $w\in W$, with $a_1
eq b_1$; write $a:=a_1$, $b:=b_1$, and assume as induction hypothesis that part (1) holds for all elements of length at most $q-1$. Since $\mathbf b$ is reduced, $bw=b_2\cdots b_q$ has length $q-1$, so the exchange condition of [F4] applied to the reduced word $\mathbf a$ and the letter $b$ gives $bw=a_1\cdots\widehat{a_i}\cdots a_q$ for some $i\in\{1,\dots,q\}$, that is $w=b\,a_1\cdots\widehat{a_i}\cdots a_q$. Multiplying the equality $bw=a_1\cdots\widehat{a_i}\cdots a_q$ on the right by $a_qa_{q-1}\cdots a_{i+1}$ and then by $a_i$ shows that it is equivalent to $b\,a_1\cdots a_{i-1}=a_1\cdots a_i$; in particular $i
eq1$, since $i=1$ would give $b=a_1=a$, contrary to $a
eq b$. Hence $i\ge2$, and the word $(b,a_1,\dots,\widehat{a_i},\dots,a_q)$ is a reduced expression of $w$. Its tail $(a_1,\dots,\widehat{a_i},\dots,a_q)$ and the suffix $(b_2,\dots,b_q)$ are reduced expressions of the same element $bw$ of length $q-1$, so by the induction hypothesis they are braid-equivalent, and prepending the letter $b$ to both words gives the braid-equivalence of $(b,a_1,\dots,\widehat{a_i},\dots,a_q)$ with $(b,b_2,\dots,b_q)=\mathbf b$. If $i<q$, multiplying the equality $b\,a_1\cdots a_{i-1}=a_1\cdots a_i$ on the right by $a_{i+1}\cdots a_{q-1}$ shows that the words $(b,a_1,\dots,\widehat{a_i},\dots,a_{q-1})$ and $(a_1,\dots,a_{q-1})$ are reduced expressions of the same element $a_1\cdots a_{q-1}$ of length $q-1$, so by the induction hypothesis they are braid-equivalent, and appending the letter $a_q$ to both gives the braid-equivalence of $(b,a_1,\dots,\widehat{a_i},\dots,a_q)$ with $\mathbf a$; combining the two braid-equivalences, $\mathbf a$ is braid-equivalent to $\mathbf b$. Thus either $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are braid-equivalent, or $i=q$, in which case $w=b\,a_1\cdots a_{q-1}$ and $(b,a_1,\dots,a_{q-1})$ is braid-equivalent to $\mathbf b$. [F1, F3, F4]

2.1 **The iteration.** Keep the setup of step 1.3 and assume now that the two words are not braid-equivalent. For $j\in\{1,\dots,q\}$ let $\sigma(j)$ be the $q$-letter word consisting of the alternating word of length $q-j+1$ ending in $a$ followed by the letters $a_2,a_3,\dots,a_j$. Thus $\sigma(q)=(a_1,\dots,a_q)=\mathbf a$ and $\sigma(q-1)=(b,a,a_2,\dots,a_{q-1})$; let $C_j$ denote the braid class of $\sigma(j)$ when $\sigma(j)$ is reduced. I claim that for every $p\in\{0,\dots,q-2\}$: either $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are braid-equivalent, or $\sigma(j)$ is reduced, represents $w$, and $C_j$ is the class of $\mathbf a$ when $j-q$ is even and the class of $\mathbf b$ when $j-q$ is odd, for every $j\in\{q-p-1,\dots,q\}$. For $p=0$ this is step 1.3: either the words are braid-equivalent, or $w=b\,a_1\cdots a_{q-1}$ and the word $\sigma(q-1)=(b,a_1,\dots,a_{q-1})$ is braid-equivalent to $\mathbf b$, while $\sigma(q)=\mathbf a$, which is the assertion for $j=q-1,q$. For the induction step, suppose the claim known for $p-1$, so that $\sigma(q-p)$ and $\sigma(q-p+1)$ are reduced words for $w$; apply step 1.3 to this pair of words. If they are braid-equivalent, then their classes coincide and, since $q-p$ and $q-p+1$ have opposite parity, the known class rule forces the classes of $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ to coincide, and we are done. Otherwise the second alternative of step 1.3 holds for the pair, which says that deleting the last letter of $\sigma(q-p)$ and prepending the first letter of $\sigma(q-p+1)$ yields a word that is reduced, represents $w$, and is braid-equivalent to $\sigma(q-p+1)$. Now $\sigma(q-p)$ is the alternating word of length $p+1$ ending in $a$ followed by $a_2,\dots,a_{q-p}$, so deleting its last letter leaves the alternating word of length $p+1$ ending in $a$ followed by $a_2,\dots,a_{q-p-1}$; the first letter of $\sigma(q-p+1)$ is the first letter of the alternating word of length $p$ ending in $a$, which differs from the first letter of the alternating word of length $p+1$ ending in $a$, so prepending it produces the alternating word of length $p+2$ ending in $a$ followed by $a_2,\dots,a_{q-p-1}$, which is exactly $\sigma(q-p-1)$. Hence $\sigma(q-p-1)$ is reduced, represents $w$, and lies in the class of $\sigma(q-p+1)$; since $q-p-1$ and $q-p+1$ have the same parity, this agrees with the claimed class rule and the claim holds for $p$. [F3, step 1.3]

3.1 **The final phase.** Assume the claim of step 2.1 with $p=q-2$, and assume that $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are not braid-equivalent; then every $\sigma(j)$ for $j\in\{1,\dots,q\}$ is a reduced word for $w$ whose class is the class of $\mathbf a$ when $j-q$ is even and the class of $\mathbf b$ when $j-q$ is odd. In particular $\sigma(1)$ is the alternating word of length $q$ ending in $a$, and $\sigma(2)$ is the alternating word of length $q-1$ ending in $a$ followed by the single letter $a_2$. Write $v$ for the value of the alternating word of length $q-1$ ending in $a$ and $\varepsilon$ for the letter with which the alternating word of length $q$ ending in $a$ begins; then the word $\sigma(1)$ has value $\varepsilon v$ and $\sigma(2)$ has value $v a_2$, and since both represent $w$ one has $\varepsilon v=v a_2$, that is $a_2=v^{-1}\varepsilon v$. So $a_2$ is conjugate to $\varepsilon\in\{a,b\}$ by the element $v$, which lies in the dihedral subgroup $\langle a,b\rangle$; hence $a_2\in\langle a,b\rangle$, and since $a_2\in S$, step 1.1 gives $a_2\in\{a,b\}$. The letter $a_2$ cannot be $a$: the word $\sigma(2)$ would then end in two equal letters $a,a$, and deleting that pair would express $w$ by a word shorter than $q=\ell(w)$, so $\sigma(2)$ would not be reduced. Hence $a_2=b$, so $\sigma(2)$ is the alternating word of length $q$ ending in $b$; of the two alternating words of length $q$ in $\{a,b\}$, $\sigma(1)$ ends in $a$ and $\sigma(2)$ ends in $b$. To see that this forces $q=m$, compare the values of $\sigma(1)$ and $\sigma(2)$ in the dihedral group $\langle a,b\rangle$, whose elements are the powers of $r=ab$; if $q$ is even these values are $(r^{-1})^{q/2}$ and $r^{q/2}$, equal exactly when $r^q=1$, and if $q$ is odd they are $r^{(q-1)/2}a$ and $r^{-(q-1)/2}b$, equal exactly when $r^{q-1}=r^{-1}$, that is $r^q=1$. Since $\sigma(1)$ and $\sigma(2)$ represent the same element, $r^q=1$; when $m=\infty$ no positive power of $r$ is $1$ by [F3], so this alternative cannot occur and $m<\infty$, and then by minimality of the order $m$ one has $q\ge m$. Conversely $q\le m$: by [F3] the prefix reflections of the reduced word $\sigma(1)$ are pairwise distinct, while the closed form of [F3] for alternating words gives $r_{i+m}=r_i$ for these reflections (here $(ab)^m=1$ because $m<\infty$), so $q>m$ would make the reflections at positions $1$ and $1+m$ coincide, a contradiction. Hence $q=m$. Finally, the two words $\sigma(1)$ and $\sigma(2)$ are the two alternating words of length $m$, so one is obtained from the other by the single replacement of the alternating block of length $m$ by the other alternating word of the same length; they are braid-equivalent, hence in the same class, but by the class rule their classes are the classes of $\mathbf a$ and of $\mathbf b$ respectively, so $\mathbf a$ and $\mathbf b$ are braid-equivalent, against the assumption. [F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 **Conclusion.** Part (1) follows by strong induction on $q=\ell(w)$: for $q\le1$ two reduced words for $w$ coincide, and for $q\ge2$, reduced words with the same first letter are handled by the induction hypothesis applied to their tails, while reduced words with different first letters are handled by steps 1.3, 2.1 and 3.1, which produce braid-equivalence in every case. For part (2), let $\mathbf c=(c_1,\dots,c_k)$ be a word with value $w$. If $\mathbf c$ is reduced, no sequence of braid moves and deletions of consecutive equal pairs can shorten it: braid moves preserve the value and the length by step 1.2, deleting a consecutive pair preserves the value, and a shorter word for $w$ would contradict $k=\ell(w)$. Conversely, if $\mathbf c$ is not reduced, we show by induction on $k$ that it can be shortened; for $k\le1$ the word is reduced, so $k\ge2$, and if the suffix $(c_2,\dots,c_k)$ can be shortened, the same sequence shortens the whole word. Otherwise the suffix is M-reduced, so by induction on $k$ it is reduced, with value $w'$ and $\ell(w')=k-1$. Since $w=c_1w'$ has length at most $k-1<\ell(w')+1$, the length laws of [F4] give $\ell(c_1w')=\ell(w')-1=k-2$, and the exchange condition of [F4] applied to the reduced word $(c_2,\dots,c_k)$ and the letter $c_1$ gives $c_1w'=c_2\cdots\widehat{c_j}\cdots c_k$ for some $j$, so that $w'=c_1c_2\cdots\widehat{c_j}\cdots c_k$ is a reduced expression of $w'$ of length $k-1$ beginning with $c_1$. By part (1) it is braid-equivalent to $(c_2,\dots,c_k)$, and prepending $c_1$ to both words exhibits a sequence of braid moves taking $\mathbf c=(c_1,c_2,\dots,c_k)$ to $(c_1,c_1,c_2,\dots,\widehat{c_j},\dots,c_k)$, which the deletion of the consecutive pair $c_1,c_1$ shortens. Hence a word is reduced if and only if it is M-reduced. [F1, F3, F4, step 1.2, step 3.1] ∎

citations.quote: **The representation and the exact dihedral orders.** The assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ respects every defining relator of $W$ and induces a unique homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ with $\sigma(s)=\sigma_s$.

source_paragraphs: Let $(W,S)$ be a Coxeter system of finite type, with $S$ finite; finite type means $W$ is finite ([[def-cg-coxeter-diagram-components-and-finite-type]] (4)). Use the right and left weak orders, covers, meets and joins of [[def-cg-left-right-weak-order-and-descents]], and the inversion sets $N(w)=\{\alpha\in\Phi_+:\rho(w)\alpha\in\Phi_-\}$ of [[def-cg-geometric-inversion-set]]. For $J\subseteq S$, write $w=w_Jd$ for the unique length-additive factorization with $w_J\in W_J$ and $d\in{}^JW$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_Jw$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3), [[def-cg-parabolic-quotient-and-two-sided-minima]] (2)); call $w_J$ the $W_J$-prefix of $w$. Put $\Phi_{J,+}:=\Phi_J\cap\Phi_+$, where $\Phi_J=\Phi\cap V_J$ and $V_J=\operatorname{span}\{e_s:s\in J\}$ ([[thm-cg-parabolic-intersections-and-coset-factorization]] (2)). Let $w_0$ and $w_0(J)$ be the longest elements of $W$ and $W_J$, respectively ([[thm-cg-finite-parabolic-longest-element-and-opposition]]).

[F6] Every right coset $W_Jw$ has a unique minimal representative $d$, characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$; every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=ud$ with $u\in W_J$ and this $d$, $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$, and $\ell(vd)=\ell(v)+\ell(d)$ for every $v\in W_J$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3)).

[F12] The support $S(w)$ is independent of the reduced expression, and $w\in W_J$ if and only if $S(w)\subseteq J$; hence every reduced expression of an element of $W_J$ uses only letters of $J$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (1)).
[F14] For each $J\subseteq S$, $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system and its intrinsic length agrees with the ambient length on $W_J$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2)).
source_use_steps: 1.1 Finite setup and notation. By [F1], $W$ is finite, and each $W_J$ is finite. Fix $J\subseteq S$ and $w\in W$. Write $w=w_Jd$ for its unique length-additive factorization, with $d$ minimal in $W_Jw$ by [F6]; $w_J$, $W_J$, $\Phi_{J,+}$, $N$, $w_0$ and $w_0(J)$ have the meanings fixed in the Statement and [F7]-[F9],[F15]. [F1, F6, F7, F8, F9, F15, given]

1.2 The minimal representative above the parabolic factor. Let $L:=\ell(w_0)$ and $L_J:=\ell(w_0(J))$. By [F5], $q:=w_0(J)w_0$ has length $L-L_J$. For each $s\in J$, [F15] gives $\ell(sw_0(J))=L_J-1$ and [F5] gives $\ell(sq)=\ell(sw_0(J)w_0)=L-(L_J-1)=\ell(q)+1$. Thus $q$ has no left descent in $J$ and is the minimal representative of $W_Jw_0$ by [F6]. Since $w_0(J)^2=1$ by [F15], $w_0=w_0(J)q$. Therefore $x:=zq=z\,w_0(J)\,w_0$ is the length-additive parabolic factorization with prefix $z$, and $\ell(x)=\ell(z)+L-L_J$. Also $N(w_0(J)^{-1})\subseteq\Phi_{J,+}$ by [F8],[F16], and its cardinality is $L_J=|\Phi_{J,+}|$ by [F16],[F23]; consequently $w_0(J)$ sends every positive subsystem root to a negative subsystem root. [F5, F6, F8, F15, F16, F23]

2.1 Prefix inversion set. Choose a reduced expression $w_J=s_1\cdots s_k$ with letters in $J$ (available by [F12]) and a reduced expression $d=s_{k+1}\cdots s_n$. Their concatenation is reduced by [F6]. The prefix roots for indices $i\le k$ in the formula [F16] are the prefix roots of $N(w_J^{-1})$ and lie in $\Phi_{J,+}$, because their reflections are words in $J$ and [F8] identifies the roots of $W_J$. If a suffix index $i>k$ had prefix root $\alpha_i\in\Phi_{J,+}$, then $t_{\alpha_i}\in W_J$ by [F22]. Write $w=p s_i r$ with $p=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}$ and $r=s_{i+1}\cdots s_n$. By [F16], $\alpha_i=\rho(p)e_{s_i}$, and [F25] gives $t_{\alpha_i}=p s_i p^{-1}$; hence $t_{\alpha_i}w=p r=w_Jd'$, where $d'$ is represented by the suffix word with $s_i$ deleted and has length at most $\ell(d)-1$. Since $t_{\alpha_i}\in W_J$, $t_{\alpha_i}w\in W_Jw=W_Jd$, so $d'=w_J^{-1}t_{\alpha_i}w\in W_Jd$. This contradicts the minimality of $d$. Thus no suffix root lies in $\Phi_{J,+}$, while all prefix roots do; the inversion formula gives $N(w^{-1})\cap\Phi_{J,+}=N(w_J^{-1})$. [F6, F8, F12, F16, F22, F25, step 1.1]

2.2 Inversion set of the lift. Let $x=z\,w_0(J)\,w_0$. If $\alpha\in\Phi_{J,+}$, then $\beta:=\rho(z^{-1})\alpha$ is a root of the subsystem. By step 1.2, $\rho(w_0(J))$ reverses the sign of subsystem roots, while $\rho(w_0)$ reverses the sign of every root; therefore $\rho(x^{-1})\alpha\in\Phi_-$ exactly when $\rho(z^{-1})\alpha\in\Phi_-$, so $\alpha\in N(x^{-1})$ exactly when $\alpha\in N(z^{-1})$. If $\alpha\in\Phi_+\setminus\Phi_{J,+}$, choose reduced words for $z^{-1}$ and $w_0(J)$; their letters lie in $J$ by [F12]. At every letter $r\in J$, the current root remains outside $V_J$: since $\rho(r)$ is invertible and preserves $V_J$ by [F8], it cannot send a vector outside $V_J$ into $V_J$. Thus the current root is never $e_r$, and [F17] keeps it positive. Then $\rho(w_0)$ sends the resulting positive root to a negative root by [F5], so every such $\alpha$ belongs to $N(x^{-1})$. This proves $N(x^{-1})=N(z^{-1})\cup(\Phi_+\setminus\Phi_{J,+})$. [F5, F8, F9, F11, F12, F17, step 1.2]

3.1 Greatest prefix and order-preserving projection. If $v\in W_J$, [F12] says every reduced word for $v$ uses only letters of $J$, so every prefix root of a reduced word for $v$ lies in $\Phi_{J,+}$ by [F8] and [F16]. Thus, when $v\le_R w$, the criterion [F3] and step 2.1 give $N(v^{-1})\subseteq N(w_J^{-1})$, so $v\le_R w_J$; conversely $w_J\le_R w$ by the factorization [F6] and the definition [F24]. This proves the greatest-element claim and $v\le_R w\iff v\le_R w_J$ for $v\in W_J$. If $x\le_R y$, intersect $N(x^{-1})\subseteq N(y^{-1})$ with $\Phi_{J,+}$ and apply step 2.1 to both prefixes; [F3] gives $x_J\le_R y_J$. [F3, F6, F8, F12, F16, F19, F24, step 2.1]

3.2 Cover-join clause (4)(i). Let $J=S\setminus\{s\}$ and assume the hypotheses of (i). By [F16], $N(s^{-1})=\{e_s\}$, so $e_s\in N(w^{-1})$ implies $s\le_R w$ by [F3]; also $w_J\le_R w$ by the length-additive factorization [F6] and the definition [F24]. The element $w$ is therefore a common upper bound. Suppose a strict common upper bound $u<_R w$ existed. By [F20], choose a cover predecessor $v\lessdot_R w$ with $u\le_R v$; by step 1.3 it deletes some $\alpha\in\operatorname{cov}(w)$. If $\alpha=e_s$, then $e_s
otin N(v^{-1})$, so $s
ot\le_R v$ by [F3]. If $\alpha

ot\le_R v$ by [F3]. Both cases contradict $u\le_R v$ and $s,w_J\le_R u$. Hence no strict common upper bound lies below $w$. The join $s\vee w_J$ exists by [F4], and by its least-upper-bound definition [F2] is at most $w$; it equals $w$. [F2, F3, F4, F6, F13, F16, F19, F20, F22, F24, step 2.1, step 1.3]

4.2 Meet preservation. The finite weak orders on $W$ and $W_J$ are lattices by [F4] and [F14]. For $u\in W_J$, step 3.1 gives $u\le_R v$ exactly when $u\le_R v_J$. By the meet definition [F2], for every $u\in W_J$, $u\le_R x_J\wedge y_J$ exactly when $u\le_R x_J$ and $u\le_R y_J$, exactly when $u\le_R x$ and $u\le_R y$, exactly when $u\le_R x\wedge y$, exactly when $u\le_R (x\wedge y)_J$. Both candidate meets lie in $W_J$, so antisymmetry [F19] yields $(x\wedge y)_J=x_J\wedge y_J$. [F2, F4, F14, F19, step 3.1]

5.1 Join preservation and surjectivity. Put $z:=x_J\vee y_J\in W_J$ and let $X:=z\,w_0(J)\,w_0$ be its largest lift from step 4.1. Since $x_J,y_J\le_R z$, the adjunction in step 4.1 gives $x,y\le_R X$, so $x\vee y\le_R X$ and order preservation gives $(x\vee y)_J\le_R z$. Conversely, order preservation applied to $x,y\le_R x\vee y$ gives $x_J,y_J\le_R(x\vee y)_J$, hence $z\le_R(x\vee y)_J$. The join definition [F2] makes $z$ the least upper bound of $x_J,y_J$; the two bounds and antisymmetry [F19] yield $(x\vee y)_J=z$. If $z\in W_J$, then its parabolic factorization is $z=z\cdot1$, so $z_J=z$; the projection is onto $W_J$. [F2, F3, F4, F6, F14, F19, step 3.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Cover-join clause (4)(ii): the simple root and other parabolic covers. Let $y\in W_J$ and put $z:=s\vee y$. By [F12], every reduced expression of $y$ uses letters in $J$, so [F16] and [F8] give $N(y^{-1})\subseteq\Phi_{J,+}$. Since $J=S\setminus\{s\}$, the simple basis vector $e_s$ is not in $V_J$ and hence not in $\Phi_{J,+}$. Thus $N(s^{-1})\cap\Phi_{J,+}=\emptyset$ by [F16], and step 2.1 gives $N(s_J^{-1})=\emptyset=N(1)$. The inversion criterion [F3] and partial order [F19] imply $s_J=1$. Hence projection-join preservation in step 5.1 gives $z_J=y$. Further, $s
ot\le_R y$, because $N(s^{-1})=\{e_s\}$ by [F16] and $e_s
otin\Phi_{J,+}$; thus $y<_R z$. Choose a cover predecessor $v\lessdot_R z$ with $y\le_R v$ by [F20]. Since $s\le_R z$, [F16] and [F3] give $e_s\in N(z^{-1})$; if $e_s
otin\operatorname{cov}(z)$, step 1.3 says no cover predecessor deletes it, so $e_s\in N(v^{-1})$ and $s\le_R v$, contradicting that $z$ is the join of $s$ and $y$. Hence $e_s\in\operatorname{cov}(z)$. If $\alpha\in\operatorname{cov}(z)\setminus\{e_s\}$ and $t_\alpha
otin W_J$, then $\alpha
otin\Phi_{J,+}$ by [F22]. The predecessor $v=t_\alpha z$ deletes only $\alpha$ by step 1.3, so it retains $N(y^{-1})\subseteq N(z^{-1})\cap\Phi_{J,+}$ and retains $e_s$; hence $y,s\le_R v<_R z$, again contradicting the join. Therefore every such $t_\alpha$ lies in $W_J$. [F2, F3, F8, F12, F13, F16, F19, F20, F22, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 1.3]

7.1 The cover roots inside the parabolic. Since $z_J=y$ by step 5.1, write $z=yd$ with $d$ the minimal right-coset representative. If $\alpha\in\operatorname{cov}(z)\setminus\{e_s\}$, step 6.1 gives $t_\alpha\in W_J$, so $\alpha\in\Phi_{J,+}$ by [F22]. Since $W_Jt_\alpha z=W_Jz$, $d$ remains the minimal representative of this coset by [F6], and $t_\alpha z=(t_\alpha y)d$ is the length-additive parabolic factorization. Thus its prefix is $t_\alpha y$; as $t_\alpha z$ covers $z$, lengths give $\ell(t_\alpha y)=\ell(y)-1$. Intersecting the deletion formula of step 1.3 with $\Phi_{J,+}$ and using step 2.1 gives $N((t_\alpha y)^{-1})=N(y^{-1})\setminus\{\alpha\}$. By [F3], $t_\alpha y\le_R y$, and the length difference one makes it a cover by [F20]; hence $\alpha\in\operatorname{cov}(y)$. Conversely let $\alpha\in\operatorname{cov}(y)$. By [F12], a reduced word for $y$ uses only letters in $J$; its prefix roots have the form in [F16] and lie in $\Phi_{J,+}$ by [F8], so $t_\alpha\in W_J$ by [F22]. Put $y':=t_\alpha y$ and $z':=s\vee y'$. Since $y'=ys$ with $\ell(y')=\ell(y)-1$, [F24] gives $y'<_R y$; therefore $z=s\vee y$ is an upper bound of $s,y'$ and [F2] gives $z'=s\vee y'\le_R z$. Step 5.1 gives $z'_J=y'$ and $z_J=y$, so $z'\ne z$; hence $z'<_R z$. Choose $v\lessdot_R z$ with $z'\le_R v$ by [F20], and let $\beta\in\operatorname{cov}(z)$ be its deleted root from step 1.3. Since $s,y'\le_R v$, if $\beta\notin N(y^{-1})$ then $N(y^{-1})\subseteq N(v^{-1})$ and $y\le_R v$, contradicting the join. If $\beta\in N(y^{-1})$, then step 1.3 gives $N((y')^{-1})=N(y^{-1})\setminus\{\alpha\}$; because $y'\le_R v$, the deleted root $\beta$ cannot lie in this latter set, so $\beta=\alpha$. Therefore $v=t_\alpha z$ and $\alpha\in\operatorname{cov}(z)$. This proves $\operatorname{cov}(z)=\operatorname{cov}(y)\cup\{e_s\}$. [F2, F3, F6, F8, F12, F13, F16, F19, F20, F22, F24, step 2.1, step 5.1, step 1.3, step 6.1]

citations.quote: Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies $$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$ Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$.
For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression
Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$

source_paragraphs: **(2) Point stabilizers are spherical parabolics.** Every point of $\Sigma$ lies in the relative interior of exactly one cell $q=wW_T$ ([[thm-cg-davis-complex-cell-incidence-and-stabilizers]] (2)); let $\dot q$ be the unique minimum-length representative of $q$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (3)). Since $T$ is spherical, $(W_T,T)$ is a finite-type Coxeter system, and the chamber tiling of its reflection space partitions $V_T$ into relative interiors of chamber faces $w_0C^T_I$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2), [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]], [[thm-cg-finite-chamber-tiling-and-coset-face-identification]] (1),(3),(4)). Thus if $y$ is in the relative interior of $q$ and has coordinate $y'\in\operatorname{relint}(w_0C^T_I)$ in the $\dot q$-chart, where $w_0\in W_T$ and $I\subseteq T$, then $$\operatorname{Stab}_W(y)=(\dot q w_0)W_I(\dot q w_0)^{-1}$$ ([[thm-cg-davis-complex-cell-incidence-and-stabilizers]] (2)). Because $I\subseteq T$ and $W_T$ is finite, $W_I\le W_T$ is finite; hence this point stabilizer is a spherical parabolic and is contained in the setwise stabilizer $wW_Tw^{-1}$ of $q$.

[F7] For every spherical $T$, the restricted parabolic $(W_T,T)$ is a finite-type Coxeter system, and in its reflection space $V_T$ the relative interiors of the finite-type chamber faces $w_0C^T_I$ partition $V_T$, including the rank-zero case $T=\emptyset$ ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (2), [[def-cg-real-coxeter-form-and-reflection]], [[def-cg-canonical-reflection-homomorphism]], [[def-cg-finite-reflection-arrangement-and-spherical-chambers]], [[thm-cg-finite-chamber-tiling-and-coset-face-identification]] (1),(3),(4)).
source_use_steps: 1.3 Clause (2), the stabilizer formula. Let $q=wW_T$ be a cell and $y$ a point in its relative interior, with coordinate $y'\in C_T$ in the chart determined by $\dot q$. By [F7], there is a unique chamber face $w_0C^T_I$ whose relative interior contains $y'$, including the full chamber face and its lower-dimensional faces. The stabilizer formula of [F2] gives $\operatorname{Stab}_W(y)=(\dot q w_0)W_I(\dot q w_0)^{-1}$; since $I\subseteq T$ and $W_T$ is finite, [F3] shows this is a finite spherical parabolic contained in $\dot qW_T\dot q^{-1}=wW_Tw^{-1}$. [F2, F3, F7]

2.1 Clause (3). Let $H\le W$ be finite and choose an $H$-fixed point $c\in\Sigma$ by step 1.1; let $q=wW_T$ be its unique carrier cell by step 1.2. With $\dot q$, $y'$, $w_0$, $I$ as in step 1.3, the stabilizer formula of [F2] gives $\operatorname{Stab}_W(c)=(\dot q w_0)W_I(\dot q w_0)^{-1}$. Every $h\in H$ fixes $c$, so $H\le\operatorname{Stab}_W(c)\le\dot qW_T\dot q^{-1}=wW_Tw^{-1}$ by [F3]. Since $W_T$ is finite, this cell stabilizer is a spherical parabolic; the carrier cell $q$ is unique by step 1.2. [F2, F3, F7, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3]

3.1 Clause (4) and the Choice bookkeeping. The finite subgroup $H$, its containing spherical parabolic $wW_Tw^{-1}$ and the cell $q$ were obtained in step 2.1 with no finiteness or crystallographic hypothesis on $(W,S)$ beyond $S$ finite, so the statements hold for every finite-rank Coxeter system; the listed abstentions delimit the result. In this proof, AC is required only through [F4], the CAT(0) theorem; although [F1] has a general AC branch, step 1.1 uses its proper-space branch because [F4] gives properness, and that branch is choice-free. Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.
