source_paragraphs: [F10] Support determines standard-parabolic membership and the restricted Coxeter presentation ([[thm-hh-parabolic-minimal-representatives-and-length-additivity]] (1)–(2)).
source_use_steps: 1.4 Every finite subgroup $H$ of either affine group fixes a point: average the finite orbit $H x$ for any $x$; affine linearity makes its barycentre fixed by $H$. By [F8]'s strict closed fundamental domain, conjugate this point into $\bar A$. For $p\in\bar A$, let $T(p)$ be the types of facets containing $p$. The affine relation in [F8] gives $T(p)\subsetneq S$. The intersection formula in [F8] and support criterion [F10] show $\operatorname{Stab}(p)=W_{T(p)}$: if $w p=p$, then $p\in w\bar A\cap\bar A$, so every type in $S(w)$ is in $T(p)$, hence $w\in W_{T(p)}$; conversely every generator indexed by $T(p)$ fixes $p$. This stabilizer is finite by [F8]'s proper-parabolic clause. The face containing $p$ has a vertex $v$; all its containing facet reflections fix $v$, so $H\le W_{T(p)}\le\operatorname{Stab}(v)$. Applying the same stabilizer identity to $v$ shows $\operatorname{Stab}(v)=W_{T(v)}$, a finite proper parabolic. At a vertex $v$, the $n$ incident facets have a unique intersection, so their normals span the ambient direction space and their reflections have common fixed-point set exactly $\{v\}$. If a finite group contained $\operatorname{Stab}(v)$, its barycentre would be fixed by this stabilizer, hence would equal $v$; the group would then be contained in $\operatorname{Stab}(v)$. Thus every vertex stabilizer is maximal finite, and every maximal finite subgroup is conjugate to one. [F8, F10, algebra]

2.1 Set $N=2^n n!$ and let $n\ge3$. Deleting the endpoint $v_n$ of the $4$-edge from $\tilde B_n$ leaves the finite all-$3$ $D_n$ graph (at $n=3$, the path $A_3=D_3$). Its parabolic is the stabilizer of the opposite vertex, hence maximal finite by Step 1.4, and has order $N/2$ by Step 1.3. Deleting vertex $v_i$, $0\le i\le n$, from $\tilde C_n$ leaves two finite terminal-$4$ paths of ranks $i$ and $n-i$, interpreted as $B_1=A_1$ or rank-zero trivial blocks at the ends. Its vertex stabilizer has order $2^n i!(n-i)!$ by the restricted presentation [F10] and Step 1.3; the two blocks commute and their presented group is the direct product. At $i=0,n$ this is $N$. For $1\le i\le n-1$, $\binom ni\ge n$: the ratio $\binom n{i+1}/\binom ni=(n-i)/(i+1)$ shows the binomial coefficients increase to the middle and then decrease symmetrically, so their minimum on these indices is $\binom n1=\binom n{n-1}=n$. Hence the order is at most $N/n<N/2$. By Step 1.4 these are all maximal finite subgroup orders in $W_a(C_n)$. The two groups therefore cannot be abstractly isomorphic, since an isomorphism preserves finiteness, maximality and subgroup order. [F1, F9, F10, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

1.2 Restriction recursion: let $s$ be initial in $c$ and $u\in W$ with $s\notin S(u)$. The letters $s$ are exactly the first letters of the successive $c$-blocks, and deleting them from $c^\infty$ leaves the periodic word $(sc)^\infty$; the remainder of the $c^\infty$-scan is always in $W_{S\setminus\{s\}}$: it starts at $u$, and if $\rho\in W_{S\setminus\{s\}}$ then $a\rho\in W_{S\setminus\{s\}}$ for every selected $a\in S\setminus\{s\}$, while $s\notin D_L(\rho)$: in the factorization $\rho=ud$ of [F14] with $J=\{s\}$ one must have $d=\rho$, since otherwise $\rho=s\,d$ would give $s\in S(\rho)=\{s\}\cup S(d)$ [F14], contradicting $S(\rho)\subseteq S\setminus\{s\}$; hence $\ell(s\rho)=\ell(\rho)+1$ and $s$ is not a left descent. Therefore no $s$-letter is ever selected [F2], and the scan of the remaining letters coincides position-by-position with the $(sc)^\infty$-scan of $u$, with the same remainders; by the uniqueness in [F2] the two sorting words coincide and, since the non-$s$ letters of the $j$-th $c$-block are exactly the $j$-th $sc$-block, $T_j^{(c)}(u)=T_j^{(sc)}(u)$ for every $j$. Consequently $u$ is $c$-sortable if and only if it is $sc$-sortable, and the $sc$-sorting word for $u$ is a $c$-sorting word for $u$. [F2, F14, F16, algebra]

otin D_L(u)$ [F2]; the only positions carrying $s$ are $1,n+1,2n+1,\dots$, so the selected occurrence of $s$ lies in block $j\ge2$. Hence $s
otin T_1$ but $s\in T_j$ for some $j\ge2$, so the block sequence is not weakly decreasing and $u$ is not $c$-sortable [F16]. [F1, F2, F12, F14, F16, algebra]

Put $r_i=a_1\cdots a_i s a_i\cdots a_1$ for $0\le i\le j$. Then $r_j=t_{j+1}$. When $v$ is sortable we take its sorting word for the prefix. [F12, F14, algebra]

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix with presented group $W$, length $\ell$ and geometric representation $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]], [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]] and [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]], and let $J\subseteq S$.

1. **Support and reduction.** For every $w\in W$ the set $S(w)$ of letters occurring in a reduced expression of $w$ is independent of the reduced expression, and every word in $S$ representing $w$ can be transformed into a reduced expression by repeatedly deleting two letters (Tits reduction, using only letters already present). Consequently
$$W_J=\langle J\rangle=\{w\in W:S(w)\subseteq J\}.$$
2. **Intrinsic parabolic presentation.** Let $W_J^\ast$ be the group presented by the restricted Coxeter matrix $(J,m|_J)$ in the sense of [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The canonical homomorphism $W_J^\ast\to W_J$, $s\mapsto s$, is an isomorphism. Hence $(W_J,J)$ is a Coxeter system, its intrinsic length function $\ell_J$ agrees with the ambient length $\ell$ on $W_J$, and $W_J\cap S=J$.
3. **Minimal coset representatives.** Every right coset $W_J a:=\{ua:u\in W_J\}$ ($a\in W$, [[def-coset]]) has a unique element $d$ of minimal length; it is characterized by $\ell(sd)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$, and it satisfies
$$\ell(ud)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)\qquad\text{for all }u\in W_J .$$
Equivalently, every $w\in W$ has a unique factorization $w=u\,d$ with $u\in W_J$ and $d$ the minimal representative of the right coset $W_J d$, and then $\ell(w)=\ell(u)+\ell(d)$. By inversion ($w\mapsto w^{-1}$ preserves lengths and interchanges the two coset families $\{W_Ja\}$ and $\{aW_J\}$), every left coset $aW_J:=\{au:u\in W_J\}$ has a unique minimal element $d$, characterized by $\ell(ds)>\ell(d)$ for all $s\in J$ and satisfying $\ell(du)=\ell(d)+\ell(u)$ for all $u\in W_J$.
4. **Type A.** Let $n\ge2$, $S=\{s_1,\dots,s_{n-1}\}$ and $m(s_i,s_j):=3$ if $|i-j|=1$, $m(s_i,s_j):=2$ if $|i-j|>1$ (a Coxeter matrix of type $A_{n-1}$). Then $s_i\mapsto(i\ i+1)$ extends to an isomorphism $W\to S_n$ (the letters $1,\dots,n$ carry the library's symmetric group by the order-preserving identification with $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$, under which $(i\ i+1)$ is the adjacent transposition $(i-1\ i)$), and for every $w\in W$,
$$\ell(w)=\operatorname{inv}\bigl(\varphi(w)\bigr),$$
the inversion number of the corresponding permutation ([[def-inversions-inversion-number-and-sign]]). In particular a word in the $s_i$ is reduced if and only if its length equals the inversion number of its value.

source_use_steps: 1.5 Local sortability recursion. Put $J_s=S\setminus\{s\}$. If initial $s$ is a left descent, the greedy scan selects its first position and then scans $(scs)^\infty$ for $sw$; selected occurrences of each letter correspond after deleting this first $s$. The per-letter initial-segment condition therefore makes $w$ sortable exactly when $sw$ is $scs$-sortable. If $s$ is not a left descent, the first occurrence is omitted; sortability then forbids every later $s$, so $w\in W_{J_s}$. Conversely, for $w\in W_{J_s}$ every greedy remainder stays in $W_{J_s}$ and cannot have an outside left descent by support invariance; removing the $s$-positions gives the $sc$-scan with identical blocks. Thus in the non-descent branch $w$ is sortable exactly when it belongs to that parabolic and is $sc$-sortable. This proves the recursion used below from the local definitions and scan. [F2, F12, algebra]

source_paragraphs: [F11] [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (7): standard dihedral alternating words of length at most $m(s,t)$ are reduced in the ambient group. [[lem-cg-finite-dihedral-subsystems-and-canonical-roots]] (3) identifies the standard rank-two subgroup with the dihedral group of order $2m$. Its $2m$ elements have alternating representatives of length at most $m$. Indeed, let $A,B$ be the alternating words of length $m$ beginning with $s,t$, respectively. Since $s,t$ are involutions, the concatenation $AB^{-1}$ is alternating of length $2m$ beginning with $s$, so $AB^{-1}=(st)^m=1$ by [[lem-hh-dihedral-root-recurrence-and-root-sign]] (1),(4); hence $A=B$. Thus an alternating length-$m$ word is its longest element, and deleting its first $s$ gives a reduced length-$m-1$ alternating word starting with $t$.
source_use_steps: 2.3 Auxiliary consequence when $s\le_Ry$ and $s\ne t$. Put $z=s\vee t$, the rank-two longest element by [F9]; then $z\le_Ry$, so $sz\le_Rsy$ by [F7]. In the rank-two system $sz$ has an alternating reduced word of length $m(s,t)-1$ beginning with $t$, by [F11], so it is sortable for $ts$, the restriction of $scs$ (where $s$ is final). Parabolic restriction and the fixed-point property give $\pi_{scs}(sz)=sz$. Since $\ell(sy)<\ell(y)$, length induction gives $sz\le_R\pi_{scs}(sy)$. Both sides are not above $s$: the left because $s(sz)=z$ lengthens, the right because it is below $sy$, which is not above $s$. Apply [F7] to their left multiples to obtain $z\le_Rs\pi_{scs}(sy)=\pi_c(y)$, hence $t\le_R\pi_c(y)$. This proves the auxiliary consequence for all simple $t$ and all $c$ under the stated inductive hypotheses. [step 1.3, F3, F7, F8, F9, F11, ih]

Let $(S,m)$ be a finite Coxeter matrix, and let $K$, $E$, $(\alpha_s)_{s\in S}$, the constants $c_{st}$ and the linear maps $\sigma_s$ be as in [[def-hh-geometric-coxeter-representation-and-roots]]; let $W$ and $\ell$ be as in [[def-hh-coxeter-matrix-word-group-and-length]]. The involution, representation, signed-action and word assertions below hold for every finite $S$, including $S=\varnothing$ and $\#S=1$. Only the rank-two assertions require distinct generators.

1. **Involutions.** $\sigma_s^2=\mathrm{id}_E$ for every $s\in S$; each $\sigma_s$ is invertible, and $\ell(s)=1$.
2. **The rank-two block.** For any distinct $s,t\in S$, put $m:=m(s,t)$, $c:=c_{st}$, $P:=\operatorname{span}(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)\subseteq E$, $A:=\sigma_s\sigma_t$ and $B:=A|_P$. Then $A(P)\subseteq P$, and in the basis $(\alpha_s,\alpha_t)$,
$$B(\alpha_s)=(c^2-1)\alpha_s+c\,\alpha_t,\qquad B(\alpha_t)=-c\,\alpha_s-\alpha_t;\qquad \operatorname{tr}(B)=c^2-2,\qquad \det(B)=1 .$$
Moreover $A(v)-v\in P$ for every $v\in E$. Consequently $E=P\oplus Q$ with $Q:=\operatorname{span}\{\alpha_u:u\in S,\ u\notin\{s,t\}\}$, and for every $v=p+q$ with $p\in P$, $q\in Q$ and every $k\ge1$,
$$A^k(p+q)=B^k p+\bigl(\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{k-1}\bigr)\bigl(A(q)-q\bigr)+q .$$
3. **Exact order of the rank-two product.** For any distinct $s,t$ and the notation of (2), when $m<\infty$ put $\zeta:=\zeta_{st}$, of order $2m$, so $c=\zeta+\zeta^{-1}$; when $m=\infty$ use $c=2$, with no $\zeta$ stipulated. Then:
   (a) if $2<m<\infty$, the characteristic polynomial of $B$ is $X^2-(c^2-2)X+1=(X-\zeta^2)(X-\zeta^{-2})$ with distinct roots; $B$ is diagonalisable, $B^m=\mathrm{id}_P$, $\mathrm{id}_P+B+\cdots+B^{m-1}=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for $0<k<m$;
   (b) if $m=2$, then $c=0$ and $B=-\mathrm{id}_P$;
   (c) if $m=\infty$, then $c=2$, $B\ne\mathrm{id}_P$, $(B-\mathrm{id}_P)^2=0$, and $B^k\ne\mathrm{id}_P$ for every $k\ge1$.
   Hence $\sigma_s\sigma_t=A$ has order exactly $m$ when $m<\infty$, and infinite order when $m=\infty$; in particular $A^m=\mathrm{id}_E$ and $A^k\ne\mathrm{id}_E$ for $0<k<m$ in the finite case.
4. **The representation and the exact dihedral orders.** The assignment $s\mapsto\sigma_s$ respects every defining relator of $W$ and induces a unique homomorphism $\sigma:W\to\mathrm{GL}_K(E)$ with $\sigma(s)=\sigma_s$. Consequently, for any distinct $s,t\in S$, one has $s\ne t$ in $W$ and $st$ has order exactly $m(s,t)$ in $W$ (infinite when $m(s,t)=\infty$).
5. **The signed reflection action.** Let $T:=\{wsw^{-1}:w\in W,\ s\in S\}\subseteq W$. For $s\in S$ define $U_s:\{\pm1\}\times T\to\{\pm1\}\times T$ by
$$U_s(\varepsilon,r):=\bigl(\varepsilon\cdot(-1)^{\delta(s,r)},\ srs\bigr),$$
where $\delta(s,r)=1$ if $r=s$ and $\delta(s,r)=0$ otherwise. Then $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ for every $s$, and the assignment $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot s:=U_s(\varepsilon,r)$ extends to a well-defined **right action** of $W$ on $\{\pm1\}\times T$ (so $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot1=(\varepsilon,r)$ and $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot(wv)=((\varepsilon,r)\cdot w)\cdot v$). Indeed the only relations to check are $s^2=1$ and, for distinct $s,t$ with $m=m(s,t)<\infty$, $(st)^m=1$: $U_s^2=\mathrm{id}$ because for $r=s$ the two signs cancel while for $r\ne s$ one has $srs\ne s$ and $U_s(\varepsilon,srs)=(\varepsilon,r)$; and the alternating word $s\,t\,s\,t\cdots$ of length $2m$ acts trivially because its $2m$ prefix reflections $r_i:=w_{i-1}s_iw_{i-1}^{-1}$ (with $w_j:=s_1\cdots s_j$) satisfy $r_{i+m}=r_i$ for $1\le i\le m$ and $r_1,\dots,r_m$ are pairwise distinct, so each reflection of the dihedral subgroup $\langle s,t\rangle$ occurs exactly twice and every accumulated sign is even while the conjugating coordinate returns to $r$ because $(st)^m=1$.
6. **Prefix reflections, deletion and expression independence.** Let $(s_1,\dots,s_k)$ be a word in $S$ with value $w=s_1\cdots s_k$ and prefix reflections $r_i=s_1\cdots s_{i-1}s_is_{i-1}\cdots s_1$, and let $n(r):=\#\{i:r_i=r\}$.
   (a) If $r_i=r_j$ for some $i<j$, then $s_1\cdots\widehat{s_i}\cdots\widehat{s_j}\cdots s_k=w$: the two letters $s_i,s_j$ can be deleted.
   (b) $(-1)^{n(r)}=:\eta(r,w)$ depends only on $w$ and $r$, and the right action satisfies $(\varepsilon,r)\cdot w=(\varepsilon\,\eta(r,w),\,w^{-1}rw)$.
   (c) If the word is reduced ($k=\ell(w)$), then $n(r)\in\{0,1\}$ for every $r$, the map $i\mapsto r_i$ is injective, and the set $\Phi(w):=\{r_1,\dots,r_k\}=\{r\in T:\eta(r,w)=-1\}$ is independent of the reduced expression chosen, with $\#\Phi(w)=\ell(w)$.
7. **Ambient reducedness of dihedral words.** Let $s\ne t$, $m:=m(s,t)$, and for $q\ge1$ let $w_q$ be the value of the alternating word of length $q$ beginning with $s$. If $m<\infty$ and $q\le m$, or if $m=\infty$ and $q\ge1$, then $\ell(w_q)=q$, every word in $S$ representing $w_q$ has length at least $q$, and $w_1,\dots,w_q$ are pairwise distinct. Thus dihedral alternating words are reduced in the ambient group $W$, not merely inside $\langle s,t\rangle$.

Recursing through all inputs gives these image fibers (the indicated traces end at the base $e$): $\begin{array}{c|l|l}\pi_c(w)&\pi_c^{-1}(\pi_c(w))&\text{trace}\\e&\{e\}&\text{base}\\s_1&\{s_1\}&D_1\\s_2&\{s_2,s_2s_1\}&A_1(s_2)D_2\\s_3&\{s_3,s_3s_2,s_3s_2s_1\}&A_1(s_3)A_2(s_3)D_3\text{ for }s_3;\ A_1(s_3s_2)A_2(s_3)D_3\text{ for the other two}\\s_1s_2&\{s_1s_2\}&D_1D_2\\s_1s_3&\{s_1s_3,s_1s_3s_2,s_1s_3s_2s_1\}&D_1A_2(s_3)D_3\\s_2s_3&\{s_2s_3,s_2s_1s_3,s_2s_1s_3s_2\}&A_1(s_2s_3)D_2D_3\\s_1s_2s_1&\{s_1s_2s_1\}&D_1D_2A_3(s_1)D_1\\s_1s_2s_3&\{s_1s_2s_3\}&D_1D_2D_3\\s_2s_3s_2&\{s_2s_3s_2,s_2s_3s_2s_1,s_2s_1s_3s_2s_1\}&A_1(s_2s_3s_2)D_2D_3D_2\\s_1s_2s_1s_3&\{s_1s_2s_1s_3\}&D_1D_2D_3D_1\\s_1s_2s_3s_2&\{s_1s_2s_3s_2,s_1s_2s_3s_2s_1\}&D_1D_2D_3A_1(s_2)D_2\\s_1s_2s_1s_3s_2&\{s_1s_2s_1s_3s_2\}&D_1D_2D_3D_1D_2\\w_0&\{w_0\}&D_1D_2D_3D_1D_2A_3(s_1)D_1\end{array}$. The fibers are disjoint and their sizes sum to $24$, so the table is exhaustive and proves (ii). [F1, F6, algebra]

1.10 Put $x=s_3s_2s_1=[4,1,2,3]$ and $y=s_2s_3s_2=[1,4,3,2]$. To move $4$ from position $4$ to position $1$ in $x$ requires the adjacent swaps $s_3,s_2,s_1$ in that order, so this is its unique reduced word; $y$ is the longest element on positions $2,3,4$ and has the two reduced words $s_2s_3s_2$ and $s_3s_2s_3$. Their right weak-order prefixes intersect in $e,s_3,s_3s_2$, so $x\wedge y=s_3s_2$. The upper interval of $x$ is $\{x,xs_2,xs_3,xs_2s_3,xs_3s_2,xs_2s_3s_2\}=\{4123,4213,4132,4231,4312,4321\}$: $4123$ has right ascents $s_2,s_3$; $4213$ only $s_3$; $4132$ only $s_2$; $4231$ only $s_2$; $4312$ only $s_3$; and $4321$ none, and every upper element is reached by a sequence of such simple right ascents. For these six $q$, the data $(q,\ell(q),y^{-1}q,\ell(y^{-1}q))$ are $\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}4123&3&2143&2\\4213&4&2413&3\\4132&4&2134&1\\4231&5&2431&4\\4312&5&2314&2\\4321&6&2341&3\end{array}$. By [F7], $y\le_Rq$ exactly when $\ell(y^{-1}q)=\ell(q)-3$, so the common upper bounds are exactly $4132,4312,4321$. Since the latter two are $4132s_2$ and $4132s_2s_3$, the least common upper bound is $x\vee y=s_2s_3s_2s_1$. [F1, F2, F7, algebra]

1.12 The complete $c'$ projection recursion table, in the same $D_i,A_i(v)$ notation, is $\begin{array}{c|l|l}\pi_{c'}(w)&\pi_{c'}^{-1}(\pi_{c'}(w))&\text{trace}\\e&\{e\}&\text{base}\\s_1&\{s_1\}&D_1\\s_2&\{s_2,s_2s_1,s_2s_3,s_2s_1s_3,s_2s_1s_3s_2\}&A_1(s_2)A_3(s_2)D_2\text{ for the first two};\ A_1(s_2s_3)A_3(s_2)D_2\text{ for the last three}\\s_3&\{s_3\}&A_1(s_3)D_3\\s_1s_2&\{s_1s_2,s_1s_2s_3\}&D_1A_3(s_2)D_2\\s_1s_3&\{s_1s_3\}&D_1D_3\\s_3s_2&\{s_3s_2,s_3s_2s_1\}&A_1(s_3s_2)D_3D_2\\s_1s_2s_1&\{s_1s_2s_1,s_1s_2s_1s_3,s_1s_2s_1s_3s_2\}&D_1A_3(s_2s_1)D_2D_1\\s_1s_3s_2&\{s_1s_3s_2\}&D_1D_3D_2\\s_2s_3s_2&\{s_2s_3s_2,s_2s_3s_2s_1,s_2s_1s_3s_2s_1\}&A_1(s_2s_3s_2)D_3D_2D_3\\s_1s_2s_3s_2&\{s_1s_2s_3s_2\}&D_1D_3D_2A_1(s_3)D_3\\s_1s_3s_2s_1&\{s_1s_3s_2s_1\}&D_1D_3D_2D_1\\s_1s_2s_3s_2s_1&\{s_1s_2s_3s_2s_1\}&D_1D_3D_2D_1D_3\\w_0&\{w_0\}&D_1D_3D_2D_1D_3D_2\end{array}$. Its disjoint preimages cover all $24$ inputs, and the $s_2$-row is exactly the five-element fiber in (v). [F1, F6, algebra]
